answer_raw:
The study of the quantum properties of phonons is facilitated by a diverse array of physical platforms, ranging from superconducting electromechanical systems and surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators to optomechanical crystals and levitated nanoparticles. These platforms enable the generation, manipulation, and detection of non-classical phonon states, including Fock states, squeezed states, and entangled states, often through coupling to superconducting qubits or optical cavities.

**Superconducting Electromechanical and SAW Platforms**
A prominent class of platforms involves the integration of mechanical resonators with superconducting qubits. In silicon-on-insulator (SOI) electromechanical systems, phononic crystal electrostatic transducers have been utilized to achieve high quality factors and long decoherence times; specifically, a quality factor $Q=8\times10^6$ and a decoherence time $\tau_d=265\pm25 \mu s$ were reported, with a cooperativity of 1200 [86decbe459344a][83f0a0e47b10fe][51616df9d5443e]. Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators coupled to superconducting qubits, such as the seven-mode SAWR with a flip-chip transmon operating in the 4.44-4.59 GHz range, provide another robust interface for quantum acoustics [54b43dcca4fe19][0946ad4d653b5d][c927cf7c12b740]. In these systems, the coupling strength is a critical parameter; for instance, a SAW resonator coupled to a transmon with a 1 $\mu m$ wavelength at 4.0 GHz and 10 mK exhibited a vacuum Rabi splitting $|g_0|/2\pi=2.3\pm0.1$ MHz and a relaxation time $T_1\approx20 \mu s$ [0d5fa691554bb2][d497dbd30a0162][944f48baed3a4f][b9d421daaa7d4a][c84ae5db7413fd]. The coherence of these systems is further characterized by a Ramsey time $T_{2,Ramsey} \approx 2 \mu s$ [4f2d677a477d6f].

More recent developments include the use of fluxonium qubits coupled to mechanical resonators, where a coupling strength $g\approx2\pi\times14$ MHz was achieved with a mechanical frequency $\omega_m/2\pi\approx690$ MHz at an effective temperature $T_{eff}\sim30$ mK [49b76a1b497d07][503042f120aecd][6942824d28972d]. SAW phonon interferometers have also been employed to study quantum erasure, utilizing ~4 GHz interdigital transducers (IDTs) and 125-MHz-wide SAW mirrors [c9a68767094032][8de3d5190b685c]. Additionally, bulk acoustic wave (BAW) resonators have been used to generate multi-phonon Fock states, although the consulted records did not surface specific numerical parameters for this platform [54b43dcca4fe19]. Lithium Niobate SAW platforms have been investigated for non-reciprocal microwave acoustic waves and thermal modulation of GHz SAWs [54b43dcca4fe19].

**Optomechanical Crystals and Nanobeams**
Optomechanical crystal nanobeams represent another key platform for studying phonon quantum properties. A 3.68 GHz nanobeam with a quality factor $Q=4\times10^5$ was cooled to a mean phonon occupation number $n=0.85\pm0.04$ [628c20059803c9][20b15fb48943ca][d957bd9ef094e5]. These systems are often integrated with superconducting qubits or optical cavities to enable quantum state preparation and tomography. For example, entangled mechanical resonators have been studied using quantum state preparation and tomography techniques [Wollack et al. 2021]. Schrödinger cat states have been generated in 16-$\mu g$ mechanical oscillators [Bild et al. 2022], and deterministic macroscopic entanglement has been achieved [Kotler et al. 2020]. Non-classical correlations between photons and phonons have also been observed in these systems [Riedinger et al. 2015].

**Levitated Nanoparticles**
Optically levitated nanoparticles in vacuum offer a platform for studying phonons in a free-space environment. Cryogenic free-space setups have enabled cold damping to reach a mean phonon number $n=0.65$ with a purity of 43% [fae827aa8782cf][ad34535091e5cd][e7f2b4a968e404]. These systems allow for the study of quantum superposition of molecules beyond 25 kDa [Fein et al. 2019] and the quantum control of electron spins in rotating levitated diamonds [Jin et al. 2023]. Other levitated systems include nanodumbbell torsion balances [Ahn et al. 2018], nanorotors for ultrasensitive torque detection [Ahn et al. 2019], and nano-resonators for nanoscale electric field sensing [Zhu et al. 2022]. Scalable all-optical cold damping has been proposed for these systems [Vijayan et al. 2022], and feedback cooling has been applied to room-temperature mechanical oscillators [Guo et al. 2019].

**Integrated Phononic Circuits and Heterostructures**
Reconfigurable quantum phononic circuits utilize piezo-acoustomechanical actuators, such as $Sc_xAl_{1-x}N$, to achieve $\pm\pi$ phase shifts at a 14 MHz resonance with 71 ns switching times and 90% fidelity [f908785c44014b][9120f191899b1e][b41598cc7d8c24][a6405357d6d84f]. Semiconductor-piezoelectric heterostructures, such as $In_{0.53}Ga_{0.47}As-LiNbO_3$ with a 50 nm film and 5 $\mu m$ LN layer, have been used to study electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity, with resonant frequencies $f_1=370$ MHz and $f_2=256.6$ MHz, and a 32500X efficiency improvement [5441f50c04ee42][59f070725bcca0][4104ed642f2b42].

**Other Platforms and Phenomena**
Micromechanical membranes have been laser-cooled to the quantum backaction limit, achieving $n=0.20\pm0.02$ and a backaction noise $n_{ba}=0.18$ [88b9db0aeb1cc8][e1700cd10cf981]. Remote entanglement between micromechanical oscillators has been demonstrated [Riedinger et al. 2017], and squeezing/multimode entanglement of SAW phonons has been studied [Andersson et al. 2020]. Transduction between superconducting qubits and optical photons has been achieved [Mirhosseini et al. 2020], and optically heralded microwave photon addition has been proposed [Jiang et al. 2023]. Non-classical microwave-optical photon pairs and quantum entanglement of optical-microwave photonic qubits have also been reported [Meesala et al. 2023].

Additional platforms include 2D optomechanical crystal cavities [Ren et al. 2019], on-chip cavity optomechanical coupling [Hauer et al. 2014], and cryogenic packaging of optomechanical crystals [McKenna et al. 2019]. Pulsed excitation dynamics have been studied in optomechanical crystals [Meenehan et al. 2015]. Cavity cooling of levitated nanospheres [Delić et al. 2018] and millikelvin cooling of optically trapped microspheres [Li et al. 2011] have also been explored. Acoustic resonators with bound states in the continuum (BICs) [Deriy et al. 2021, Lyapina et al. 2015], mechanical BICs in optomechanical microcavities [Yu et al. 2022], and optomechanical crystals with BICs [Liu et al. 2022] provide unique environments for phonon trapping. Phonon trapping in the continuum with topological charges [Tong et al. 2020] and phononic integrated circuitry with spin-orbit interaction [Fu et al. 2019] have also been investigated. Yoctonewton force detection [Liang et al. 2022] and adiabatic conversion of quasi-Rayleigh/quasi-Love modes [Wang et al. 2022] are further examples of phenomena studied in these platforms.

The consulted records did not surface specific numerical details for the linear mechanical QC platform (Qiao et al. 2023) or the BAW resonator platform (Chu et al. 2018) beyond their identification as platforms for single phonon beam splitters and multi-phonon Fock states, respectively.

question: What other systems, besides photonic crystals, have demonstrated bound states in the continuum?
answer:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) have been demonstrated in a variety of physical systems beyond photonic crystals, primarily within the domains of optomechanics, acoustics, and plasmonics. While most experimental demonstrations in optics and mechanics rely on periodic structures with specific symmetries , the phenomenon has been successfully realized in discrete mechanical resonators, compact acoustic cavities, and anisotropic metasurfaces.

**Optomechanical and Mechanical Systems**
Mechanical BICs have been experimentally demonstrated in optomechanical microresonators, specifically in a wheel-shaped silicon structure with a thickness of 220 nm, where azimuthal symmetry is broken to support the state [f45adada645049]. This system exhibits mechanical BIC frequencies of 2.58 GHz, 2.80 GHz, and 3.02 GHz [183d97fd454c9e, A1, A2, A3]. The existence of these states is confirmed by optomechanical measurements in vacuum, where the radiation quality factor of specific mechanical modes, such as mode 2 at 8.2 GHz, diverges, indicating a true mechanical BIC [34, 30]. In these systems, the BICs are confined within the slab due to symmetry-induced decoupling from the acoustic continuum [d2d76764cbeceb]. Theoretical and experimental work has also identified that only the C2v symmetry group supports mechanical BICs that decouple from both transverse and longitudinal acoustic continua .

Further developments include the realization of the first 2D slab-on-substrate optomechanical crystals featuring mechanical BICs [25f02a73e127d6]. In these periodic nanostructures, mechanical BICs have been observed at frequencies such as 8 GHz , with an optomechanical coupling rate of approximately 2.5 MHz per unit cell [67ea6cb0577c04]. The effective mass of a 1 μm-size unit-cell B1-BIC mode in such a crystal is stated to be 0.51 pg [e75e82c25d57e7]. The coupling rate achieved in these optomechanical crystals is on par with that of 1D suspended optomechanical crystals [965144a0b0b85f]. Additionally, mechanical BICs have been described in systems combining microwave frequency and macroscopic size within photonic nanocrystals (PnC) [c7c27a80b13c4a]. In PnCs with 200x200 unit cells, Q factors of 5.2e3, 2.8e3, and 2.2e3 have been demonstrated [58c958eda1524d]. The paper states that for a given PnC size, resonances with higher frequencies generally exhibit larger Q factors and less external coupling, with an overall trend of increasing Q factors as device sizes increase [24, 25].

High-Q Friedrich-Wintgen BICs have also been identified in wheel-shaped resonators equipped with supporting rods [58c958eda1524d]. In such configurations, a specific mode (Mode A') becomes a Friedrich-Wintgen quasi-BIC when an anticrossing in modal frequencies and a drastic variation in Q occur near a radius of 20.8 μm [9a3395c95868bd]. The formation of these BICs is attributed to destructive interference between two dissipative mechanical modes [9a3395c95868bd]. Prior to recent experimental breakthroughs, the demonstration of BICs in an individual mechanical resonator was considered elusive .

**Acoustic Systems**
Acoustic BICs have been revealed in finitely-sized, compact acoustic resonators, including solid spheres and cylinders . In these compact resonators, the spectrum consists of radiative modes and BICs with infinitely high radiative Q factors . Specifically, the fundamental acoustic BIC in a solid sphere is identified as a quadrupole mode (l=2) rather than a dipole mode .

Beyond compact resonators, BICs have been studied in open acoustic resonators, such as 2D and 3D acoustic cavities with channels, bridging the gap between acoustic and other BIC communities . In these cavities, a quasi-BIC (QBIC) corresponding to the irrep E1u appears as a high-Q Fano resonance that collapses into a genuine BIC . At this collapse point, the transmittance drops from unit to zero in 2D cavities . A two-mode approximation has been shown to reproduce the BIC pressure field in both 2D and 3D acoustic cavities . It is noted that wave localization via full destructive interference has been experimentally realized only in microwaves .

**Plasmonic Systems**
Plasmonic BICs have been demonstrated in anisotropic metasurfaces. For in-plane electric dipole (ED) excitation, only the bright mode is excited . The near-field electric intensity of this bright mode decays much faster than that of the dark mode . The bright mode is characterized by an odd charge distribution with an in-plane dipolar moment, whereas the dark mode possesses an even charge distribution with an out-of-plane dipolar moment . The Q-factor of the quasi-BIC state in these plasmonic metasurfaces is stated to be robust against changes in the period .

**Topological and Other Aspects**
While the question focuses on systems other than photonic crystals, the notes indicate that topological charges are a significant feature in BIC systems. For instance, in 1D-periodic structures in air, BICs with specific topological charges have been demonstrated, such as two BICs on the k_x axis carrying charges q=+1 . In the lowest-frequency TE-like band of a 1D-periodic structure, off-Γ BICs with charge -1 and a BIC with charge +1 at the Γ point have been observed . A stable BIC of charge -2 at the Γ point, arising from the double degeneracy of nodal lines caused by C6v symmetry, has also been demonstrated . In square-lattice photonic crystal slabs, five BICs in the first Brillouin zone reveal vortices with topological charges of ±1 [39, 40]. Laser emission based on such BIC states is stated to generate vector beams .

The consulted records did not surface specific details regarding waveguides, microcavities, or elastic systems beyond the optomechanical and acoustic resonators described above. Additionally, while references to optical BICs in photonic crystals (e.g., Plotnik et al., 2011) are present in the literature cited within the notes, the specific experimental parameters for those photonic crystal systems are not detailed in the provided records, as the focus remains on the non-photonic-crystal systems.

question: What are the large systems in which quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated?
answer:
Based on the scientific literature in this knowledge base, quantum effects have been successfully demonstrated in a range of "large" or macroscopic systems, spanning mechanical oscillators, molecules, atomic ensembles, and superconducting circuits. Below is a comprehensive account organized by system type.

**1. Mechanical oscillators (mesoscopic to macroscopic masses)**

The most striking demonstrations of quantum effects in large systems involve mechanical resonators whose masses range from picograms to micrograms:

- **Schrödinger cat states in a 16.2-microgram mechanical oscillator** (Bild et al. 2022): This is one of the largest masses in which a non-classical superposition state has been prepared. The oscillator has a mass of 16.2 micrograms and a mechanical frequency of approximately 12 MHz. The cat state parameter reached 0.9, demonstrating a well-defined superposition of two distinct mechanical states .

- **Deterministic macroscopic entanglement of two 70-picogram mechanical drumheads** (Kotler et al. 2020): Two mechanical drumhead resonators, each with a mass of 70 picograms, were deterministically entangled using pulsed electromechanics. The entangled state exhibits a correlation of the position quadratures x₁ and x₂ and an anticorrelation of the momentum quadratures p₁ and p₂, a hallmark of two-mode squeezed (entangled) states .

- **Remote quantum entanglement between two micromechanical oscillators** (Riedinger et al. 2017): Two micromechanical oscillators separated by 1,556 nm were placed in an entangled state, with an entanglement measure of 4.0 ± 0.8 (and other reported values of 1.04 ± 0.04, 8.0 ± 1.5, and 5.0 ± 1.0 depending on the metric) .

- **Quantum ground state of a 3.68 GHz nanomechanical resonator** (O'Connell et al. 2010): This was the first measurement of an engineered mesoscopic mechanical resonator predominantly in its quantum ground state, with a phonon occupation of 0.85 ± 0.04 for a 3.68 GHz mode .

- **Laser cooling of a micromechanical membrane to the quantum backaction limit** (Peterson et al. 2015): A high-quality-factor Si₃N₄ membrane was cooled to a phonon occupation of n̄ = 0.20 ± 0.02, reaching the quantum backaction limit (n_ba = 0.18). The membrane's coupling rate to the optical field was Γ₀ = 0.18 Hz, and the thermal environment was at n₀ ≈ 10³ mechanical quanta .

- **Quantum control of a levitated nanoparticle in cryogenic free space** (Novotný et al. 2021): For the first time, quantum control of mechanical degrees of freedom was achieved without an optical resonator, using a levitated nanoparticle in a cryogenic environment. The experiment approached the optimal quantum control limit to within 30% .

- **Quantum state preparation and tomography of entangled mechanical resonators** (Wollack et al. 2021): Full quantum state tomography was performed on entangled mechanical resonators, confirming non-classical correlations.

- **Optomechanical crystal near its quantum ground state** (Meenehan et al. 2015): Pulsed excitation dynamics were studied in an optomechanical crystal resonator operating near its quantum ground state.

- **Two-dimensional optomechanical crystal cavity** (Ren et al. 2019): A 2D optomechanical crystal cavity with high quantum cooperativity was demonstrated, enabling quantum-limited optomechanical interactions.

**2. Molecules (massive quantum superposition)**

- **Quantum superposition of molecules beyond 25 kDa** (Fein et al. 2019): Matter-wave interference was demonstrated for molecules with masses exceeding 25 kDa (thousands of atoms), with 2% mass resolution. High-contrast quantum interference persisted despite the presence of thousands of electrons in the molecules. This experiment excluded regions of the Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) parameter space, testing collapse models .

- **Wave–particle duality of C₆₀ molecules** (Arndt et al. 1999): Fullerenes (C₆₀, ~720 amu) were shown to exhibit wave–particle duality through matter-wave interference, demonstrating quantum behavior in molecules of considerable size .

**3. Atomic ensembles**

- **Bose–Einstein condensation in a dilute atomic vapor** (Anderson et al. 1995): A Bose–Einstein condensate was produced in a vapor of rubidium-87 atoms confined by magnetic fields and evaporatively cooled. The condensate appeared near 170 nK at a density of 2.5 × 10¹²/cm³ and was preserved for more than 15 seconds. This is a macroscopic quantum state involving a large number of atoms in a single quantum state .

**4. Superconducting circuits and hybrid quantum systems**

- **Violation of Bell's inequality in Josephson phase qubits** (Ansmann et al. 2009): Bell's inequality was violated in a system of superconducting Josephson phase qubits, demonstrating non-local quantum correlations in a macroscopic electronic circuit .

- **Quantum acoustics with superconducting qubits** (Chu et al. 2017): A superconducting qubit was coupled to surface acoustic wave (SAW) phonons in the transition-coupling regime, achieving both fast reset and high coherence. This demonstrated quantum control of acoustic phonons in a bulk material .

- **Strong dispersive coupling between a fluxonium superconducting qubit and a mechanical resonator** (Lee et al. 2023): A fluxonium qubit was strongly coupled to a mechanical resonator, enabling quantum-limited readout and control of mechanical motion.

- **Quantum electromechanical interface for long-lived phonons** (Bozkurt et al. 2022): A quantum interface was demonstrated between superconducting qubits and long-lived mechanical phonon modes.

- **Quantum entanglement between optical and microwave photonic qubits** (Meesala et al. 2023): Entanglement was generated between optical and microwave photons using a chip-scale transducer, bridging two frequency domains.

- **Superconducting qubit to optical photon transduction** (Mirhosseini et al. 2020): A superconducting qubit was used to transduce quantum states to optical photons, enabling quantum networking.

- **Optically heralded microwave photon addition** (Jiang et al. 2023): Microwave Fock states were generated via optical heralding, demonstrating quantum state engineering in the microwave domain.

- **Quantum control of surface acoustic-wave phonons** (Satzinger et al. 2018): Individual SAW phonons were coherently controlled using superconducting qubits.

- **Multi-phonon Fock states in a bulk acoustic-wave resonator** (Chu et al. 2018): Non-classical multi-phonon states were created and controlled in a bulk acoustic-wave resonator.

- **Entangled surface acoustic phonons** (Bienfait et al. 2020): Quantum erasure was demonstrated using entangled surface acoustic phonons.

- **Squeezing and multimode entanglement of SAW phonons** (Andersson et al. 2020): Squeezed and multimode entangled states of surface acoustic wave phonons were generated.

- **Reconfigurable quantum phononic circuits** (Taylor et al. 2021): Piezo-acoustomechanical interactions were used to build reconfigurable quantum circuits for phonons.

- **Splitting phonons for mechanical quantum computing** (Qiao et al. 2023): A platform for linear mechanical quantum computing was demonstrated using phonon splitting.

- **Giant electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity** (Hackett et al. 2024): A giant phononic nonlinearity mediated by electrons in a semiconductor–piezoelectric heterostructure was observed, enabling quantum-limited phonon interactions.

- **Quantum control of electron spins in rotating levitated diamonds** (Jin et al. 2023): Berry phase and quantum control of electron spins were demonstrated in levitated diamond nanoparticles.

**5. Levitated optomechanical systems**

- **Cavity cooling of a levitated nanosphere** (Delić et al. 2018): A levitated nanosphere was cooled toward its quantum ground state using coherent scattering in an optical cavity.

- **Millikelvin cooling of an optically trapped microsphere** (Li et al. 2011): An optically trapped microsphere was cooled to millikelvin temperatures, approaching the quantum regime.

In summary, the corpus documents successful demonstrations of quantum effects in systems ranging from individual molecules (C₆₀, >25 kDa) to mechanical oscillators with masses up to 16.2 micrograms, atomic condensates of thousands of rubidium atoms, and superconducting circuits. The progression from nanoscale to microgram-scale mechanical systems, and from single molecules to multi-kilodalton molecules, represents a frontier in testing the boundaries of quantum mechanics at increasingly macroscopic scales.

question: What discoveries have been made regarding the topological charge corresponding to bound states in the continuum?
answer:
The discovery of the topological nature of bound states in the continuum (BICs) fundamentally redefined their physical interpretation, establishing them not merely as resonant states with infinite quality factors, but as topological defects in the polarization field of far-field radiation. Zhen et al. (2014) demonstrated that optical BICs correspond to vortex centers in the polarization directions of the far-field radiation . These states are characterized as topological defects of polarization directions in momentum space, where the robustness of the BICs is attributed to conserved and quantized topological charges . Specifically, these topological charges are defined by the winding number of the polarization vector; the winding number along any closed path in momentum space is equal to the sum of the topological charges of the BICs enclosed by that path . This winding number remains invariant under continuous variation of system parameters, ensuring the stability of the states .

The generation and annihilation of these topological charges are governed by strict rules; they can only be created or destroyed by making large changes in system parameters, rather than through continuous tuning . The existence of robust BICs is contingent upon the presence of vorticity in the polarization . question: If we have a lot of specialized language models, how can we combine them to build a general system that combine the abilities of different models? Can this unified model be as good as the single large LM?
answer:
**Combining Specialized Language Models: Methodologies and Architectural Strategies**

The integration of multiple specialized language models into a unified general system is primarily achieved through a paradigm known as Model MoErging, which aims to recycle expert models to create an aggregate system with improved performance or generalization . Unlike traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches that jointly train all experts from scratch, MoErging methods are distinct because they utilize specialized models trained and shared by individual contributors, enabling a decentralized model development paradigm . A central component of these methods is the creation of a router that decides which expert model(s) to use for a particular input or application, allowing for dynamic routing rather than the static combinations typically produced by standard merging methods .

Several specific architectural strategies exist for combining these models. One prominent approach is the Weight-Ensembling Mixture of Experts (WEMoE), which merges most parameters and upscales the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to dynamically integrate shared and task-specific knowledge based on the input . The key insight behind this method is the identification and separation of shared versus task-specific knowledge, which mitigates parameter interference . Another strategy involves AdapterFusion, which separates knowledge extraction from knowledge composition; it learns task-specific adapters in a first step and combines them in a separate step, enabling non-destructive exploitation of multi-task representations while keeping the base model frozen . Similarly, the Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters (MixDA) decouples Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into original pre-trained FFNs for old domains and novel domain FFNs, using a mixture-of-adapters gate to fuse knowledge dynamically . This is often implemented in a two-stage process: first training a domain adapter on unlabeled data, and then a task-specific adapter on labeled data .

AdapterSoup offers a different mechanism by adding the inference cost of a single adapter, where logit ensembling scales linearly with the number of adapters . This method relies on weight averaging of adapters trained on the same domain with different hyper-parameters, which preserves pre-trained language model (PLM) performance on new domains while obtaining strong in-domain results . Furthermore, ProMoT addresses the issue of format specialization, which is identified as a key cause of forgetting, by offloading format learning into a removable soft prompt before fine-tuning the model . This approach ensures that fine-tuning does not cause over-specialization that harms pre-existing generalization via in-context learning, largely leaving pre-trained parameters intact .

**Routing Mechanisms and Their Trade-offs**

The selection of routing mechanisms is critical in determining the efficiency and adaptability of the unified system. Routing can be categorized by frequency and granularity. Per-Step routing maximizes nuanced input adaptation, whereas Task-based routing prioritizes efficiency but assumes the task is known in advance . Per-Module routing offers fine-grained control over expert utilization, while Model-level routing makes a single routing decision to reduce overhead . However, these choices involve significant trade-offs. Per-Module routing increases complexity and can lead to unstable routing where early errors cascade, while Model-level routing assumes a single expert is globally optimal for all layers, which limits adaptability . Additionally, dense routing is computationally expensive with many experts and may degrade performance due to noise or redundancy .

The choice between sparse and dense expert selection is a trade-off between computational efficiency, routing accuracy, and desired knowledge aggregation . Classifier-based routing is best suited for data-rich scenarios with complex routing needs, but it is data-dependent and increases computational requirements . Conversely, embedding-based routers can falter in highly specialized domains, and suboptimal embeddings lead to poor routing for semantic tasks . For production environments where the task is known in advance, task-specific routing methods are ideal, but practitioners should avoid them when broad generalization is needed . Router-free methods are well-suited to applications with limited routing complexity .

**Performance Comparison: Unified Models vs. Single Large LMs**

Regarding the question of whether a unified model can be as good as a single large language model, the consulted records provide qualitative evidence of superiority over specific baselines but do not surface specific numeric results comparing the merged models directly to a single large LM of equivalent scale. The notes indicate that WEMoE consistently demonstrates superiority over state-of-the-art methods across tasks, and its performance shows an upward trend with more experts . Specifically, WEMoE with a parameter setting of l=2 consistently achieves the highest performance on clean data, while WEMoE with l=0 is comparable to AdaMerging .

AdapterFusion has been shown to outperform both full fine-tuning and multi-task learning, improving upon methods that have simultaneous access to all tasks during pretraining . This is significant because multi-task learning models often overfit on low-resource tasks and underfit on high-resource tasks . AdapterSoup consistently improves performance on new domains without extra training, with text clustering providing the best performance across all domains for choosing adapter models . However, the consulted records did not surface specific numerical benchmarks (e.g., accuracy percentages or loss values) that directly quantify the gap between these unified systems and a single, monolithic large language model.

**Limitations and Challenges**

Despite the benefits, combining specialized models presents several challenges. Interference between parameters of different models can substantially deteriorate performance . Existing merging methods often seek a static optimal solution in the original parameter space and do not introduce new parameters, which limits adaptability to the unique requirements of each instance . Weight interpolation poses challenges when merging models with diverse structures . Furthermore, MoE-based methods introduce additional parameters compared to a single pre-trained model .

In the context of AdapterSoup, uniform averaging is worse than clustered approaches due to negative interference between adapters on unrelated domains . The conclusions of AdapterSoup are supported only by evidence on language models with C4 textual domains, and there is no experimental evidence for its effectiveness with other model types besides adapters . Additionally, average cosine similarity is not suitable for heterogeneous data like Reuters . While a hierarchy adapter outperforms AdapterSoup, it is significantly more expensive . Finally, routing on both MLPs and attention modules increases compute and memory usage, and the marginal gain may not justify the cost .

answer_raw:
**Combining Specialized Language Models: Methodologies and Architectural Strategies**

The integration of multiple specialized language models into a unified general system is primarily achieved through a paradigm known as Model MoErging, which aims to recycle expert models to create an aggregate system with improved performance or generalization [492f2d2964448f]. Unlike traditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches that jointly train all experts from scratch, MoErging methods are distinct because they utilize specialized models trained and shared by individual contributors, enabling a decentralized model development paradigm [d8ab583bcf17b4, ff59f3350e438e]. A central component of these methods is the creation of a router that decides which expert model(s) to use for a particular input or application, allowing for dynamic routing rather than the static combinations typically produced by standard merging methods [b84a4bb19f261c, 894a735663617c].

Several specific architectural strategies exist for combining these models. One prominent approach is the Weight-Ensembling Mixture of Experts (WEMoE), which merges most parameters and upscales the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to dynamically integrate shared and task-specific knowledge based on the input [5fa67623ff6e34]. The key insight behind this method is the identification and separation of shared versus task-specific knowledge, which mitigates parameter interference [b3845340190284]. Another strategy involves AdapterFusion, which separates knowledge extraction from knowledge composition; it learns task-specific adapters in a first step and combines them in a separate step, enabling non-destructive exploitation of multi-task representations while keeping the base model frozen [6ccc0777b2e832, d98fa680622976, 61f3e87180c2b2, 282e33862c3e1f]. Similarly, the Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters (MixDA) decouples Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into original pre-trained FFNs for old domains and novel domain FFNs, using a mixture-of-adapters gate to fuse knowledge dynamically [c39f2ce752fc2e, 177a9334dac7a0]. This is often implemented in a two-stage process: first training a domain adapter on unlabeled data, and then a task-specific adapter on labeled data [b5f5eabdcffabf].

AdapterSoup offers a different mechanism by adding the inference cost of a single adapter, where logit ensembling scales linearly with the number of adapters [c0734308fb4218]. This method relies on weight averaging of adapters trained on the same domain with different hyper-parameters, which preserves pre-trained language model (PLM) performance on new domains while obtaining strong in-domain results [4cce2d7ee9bd08]. Furthermore, ProMoT addresses the issue of format specialization, which is identified as a key cause of forgetting, by offloading format learning into a removable soft prompt before fine-tuning the model [7ed691fbfa62de, f6451397e4523a]. This approach ensures that fine-tuning does not cause over-specialization that harms pre-existing generalization via in-context learning, largely leaving pre-trained parameters intact [e4dad5c45644ea, ee3332b5627e6e].

**Routing Mechanisms and Their Trade-offs**

The selection of routing mechanisms is critical in determining the efficiency and adaptability of the unified system. Routing can be categorized by frequency and granularity. Per-Step routing maximizes nuanced input adaptation, whereas Task-based routing prioritizes efficiency but assumes the task is known in advance [f08e7ea40cf212, 49d9846c054251]. Per-Module routing offers fine-grained control over expert utilization, while Model-level routing makes a single routing decision to reduce overhead [35fbbe36bd5276, bf45673db9edb9]. However, these choices involve significant trade-offs. Per-Module routing increases complexity and can lead to unstable routing where early errors cascade, while Model-level routing assumes a single expert is globally optimal for all layers, which limits adaptability [47e2082f4a93ba, ca410d009f0bda]. Additionally, dense routing is computationally expensive with many experts and may degrade performance due to noise or redundancy [16f3fa024f8464].

The choice between sparse and dense expert selection is a trade-off between computational efficiency, routing accuracy, and desired knowledge aggregation [28094549f1db42]. Classifier-based routing is best suited for data-rich scenarios with complex routing needs, but it is data-dependent and increases computational requirements [39f75920a320fc, bf7363df9977f4, 7af818524722bd]. Conversely, embedding-based routers can falter in highly specialized domains, and suboptimal embeddings lead to poor routing for semantic tasks [ce3da67bdc1579, ff73ab04c2e235]. For production environments where the task is known in advance, task-specific routing methods are ideal, but practitioners should avoid them when broad generalization is needed [40335bfa158194, c4a428f6459e86, 5e61f708f03b61]. Router-free methods are well-suited to applications with limited routing complexity [8eba84e5a4a26f].

**Performance Comparison: Unified Models vs. Single Large LMs**

Regarding the question of whether a unified model can be as good as a single large language model, the consulted records provide qualitative evidence of superiority over specific baselines but do not surface specific numeric results comparing the merged models directly to a single large LM of equivalent scale. The notes indicate that WEMoE consistently demonstrates superiority over state-of-the-art methods across tasks, and its performance shows an upward trend with more experts [8ce4e2617a4348, 04d3b471ae35d3]. Specifically, WEMoE with a parameter setting of l=2 consistently achieves the highest performance on clean data, while WEMoE with l=0 is comparable to AdaMerging [ce65a145785f3c, 48210150b393a9].

AdapterFusion has been shown to outperform both full fine-tuning and multi-task learning, improving upon methods that have simultaneous access to all tasks during pretraining [f8c6b24a29d2c6, 94964a05b959f2, dbb842215875b1]. This is significant because multi-task learning models often overfit on low-resource tasks and underfit on high-resource tasks [4c067dfc4b84ff]. AdapterSoup consistently improves performance on new domains without extra training, with text clustering providing the best performance across all domains for choosing adapter models [0fc9565df8c88c, 0279150acfed74]. However, the consulted records did not surface specific numerical benchmarks (e.g., accuracy percentages or loss values) that directly quantify the gap between these unified systems and a single, monolithic large language model.

**Limitations and Challenges**

Despite the benefits, combining specialized models presents several challenges. Interference between parameters of different models can substantially deteriorate performance [2b1958113ca2dc]. Existing merging methods often seek a static optimal solution in the original parameter space and do not introduce new parameters, which limits adaptability to the unique requirements of each instance [4757c5eb1ba6f0, fc9223414d1446, 6c5371d29e64a4]. Weight interpolation poses challenges when merging models with diverse structures [44f8f17f4ddae1]. Furthermore, MoE-based methods introduce additional parameters compared to a single pre-trained model [ab4406747119ae].

In the context of AdapterSoup, uniform averaging is worse than clustered approaches due to negative interference between adapters on unrelated domains [49ea97936f8968]. The conclusions of AdapterSoup are supported only by evidence on language models with C4 textual domains, and there is no experimental evidence for its effectiveness with other model types besides adapters [32, 2d7869fe2920dd]. Additionally, average cosine similarity is not suitable for heterogeneous data like Reuters [4d40bd52ca747a]. While a hierarchy adapter outperforms AdapterSoup, it is significantly more expensive [0e48a439c44303]. Finally, routing on both MLPs and attention modules increases compute and memory usage, and the marginal gain may not justify the cost [279d97da999288].

question: What are ways to modulate the gigahertz surface acoustic waves?
answer:
Based on the scientific literature in this knowledge base, there are several distinct ways to modulate gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs), spanning thermal, electrical, quantum, mechanical, and nonlinear approaches:

**1. Thermal Modulation (Thermo-Acoustic Modulation)**
Shao et al. (2022) demonstrated thermal modulation of GHz SAWs on lithium niobate (LN) substrates [Thermal_Modulation_of_Gigahertz_Surface_Acoustic_Waves_on_Lithium_Niobate]. The mechanism leverages the temperature dependence of LN's elastic constants to control the phase velocity of the acoustic wave [253879490f9f90]. Key results include:
- Phase changes exceeding 720° with only 2.6 dB of heater power on bulk LN, and >720° with 0.52 dB on LN-on-sapphire (LNSa) [24e2c027eafab6, cc1f5ef63ad0c3]
- 3-dB modulation bandwidths of 18 Hz (bulk LN) and 120 Hz (LNSa) [8deb32f6788410, e76c8b301bce66]
- Rise/fall times of 896/657 ms (bulk LN) and 313/212 ms (LNSa) [5f5b96ffce5b5e, 52411a7b555c03, f5c9a4704b0d57, 1f5f9544aae7aa]
- The modulation is phase-only: S21 amplitudes are unaffected by the heater [5908f01461466c]
- Thermo-acoustic modulators offer larger tuning range and require smaller voltages compared to electro-acoustic modulators [bfb62eaf05bd55]
- An acoustic Mach-Zehnder interferometer configuration enables amplitude modulation [70b6cd8f085b09]

**2. Electrical (Electro-Acoustic) Modulation**
Shao et al. (2021) demonstrated electrical control of SAWs via the electro-acoustic effect, where an applied electric field changes the elastic constants of the substrate [Electrical_Control_of_Surface_Acoustic_Waves]. Key features:
- The electro-acoustic effect is a parametric process valid at both room and millikelvin temperatures [ad7629f2454918]
- Confining the acoustic wave to a wavelength-scale waveguide (10 μm slot) with modulation electrodes enables strong modulation [a8123592fbdc8b, d8ccfc1c8fced5]
- Demonstrated phase and amplitude modulation, as well as an acoustic frequency shifter [0b771e85c233b0]
- Reconfigurable nonreciprocal modulation by tailoring phase matching [b75b8093ebfac7]
- Half-wave voltages of 53 V and 135 V; peak transmission at 2.532 GHz [3abe7acd990e54, 69accd53342cb2, b43c8c4cf40523]
- Propagation loss: 17 dB/cm at 300 K, 5 dB/cm at LN temperature, <1 dB/cm at 1.3 K [659602ecaa4606, 79fa00fc3fa8fd, 18fcb8f8b7c2f3]
- A key limitation: bulk components show small phase changes due to the weak electro-acoustic effect, motivating the waveguide confinement approach 
- Advantages over thermal: low-temperature compatibility and faster modulation speed [c3060f1eec396a]

**3. Quantum Control via Superconducting Qubits**
Satzinger et al. (2018) demonstrated quantum control of 4.0 GHz SAW phonons (wavelength 1 μm) at ~10 mK using a superconducting qubit coupled via a SQUID tunable coupler [Quantum_control_of_surface_acoustic-wave_phonons]. Key results:
- Coupling strength |g₀|/2π tunable from 2.3 ± 0.1 MHz up to 7.3 ± 0.1 MHz, a ratio of 300 [b9d421daaa7d4a, 489d60eebf93bf, f6ff310d8d9b92]
- Controllable generation of resonator Fock states [2643355475f23d]
- Adjusting g₀ away from zero shortens qubit lifetime (Purcell effect) [95a2b1bbab950a]

**4. Adiabatic Mode Conversion**
Wang et al. (2022) demonstrated adiabatic conversion between gigahertz quasi-Rayleigh and quasi-Love modes using a tapered phononic waveguide that exploits the anisotropic elastic properties of the substrate [Adiabatic_conversion_between_gigahertz_quasi-Rayleigh_and_quasi-Love_modes_for_p]. Key features:
- Nearly perfect mode conversion by adiabatically changing the wave number along the waveguide [321e7723365f1e]
- The quasi-Love mode has in-plane displacement, minimizing damping in air/liquid environments [8d7a2da85d0666]
- Conversion efficiency depends critically on adiabaticity (dw/dx must be small enough) [d7a1134eecd3a0]
- Mode coupling is mainly caused by the anisotropic substrate [9f72a5d58cd24e]

**5. Non-Reciprocal PT-Symmetric Modulation**
Shao et al. (2020) demonstrated nonreciprocal transmission of microwave acoustic waves in a nonlinear parity-time (PT)-symmetric system [Non-reciprocal_transmission_of_microwave_acoustic_waves_in_nonlinear_parity_time]. Key features:
- Leverages the strong piezoelectricity of LN to achieve fully tunable gain, loss, and nonlinearity of SAWs via an external circuit [f7fd6ea77b82d5]
- A negative-resistance circuit provides nonlinear gain with a tunable operating point [a55e5c1581484b]
- Saturation nonlinearity breaks time-reversal symmetry, enabling nonreciprocal transmission [cf8843d10b1d50]
- A 30-groove Bragg mirror provides stronger coupling, placing the system in the broken-PT regime [4c5a67aabcae83]

**6. Electron-Mediated Phononic Nonlinearity (Frequency Conversion)**
Hackett et al. (2024) demonstrated giant electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity in semiconductor-piezoelectric heterostructures [Giant_electron-mediated_phononic_nonlinearity_in_semiconductor_piezoelectric_het]. Key features:
- Phononic frequency conversion (sum-frequency and difference-frequency generation) enhanced by orders of magnitude via heterogeneous integration of high-mobility semiconductor films [880070cb5c7a09, 9306bfc2ad2d6c]
- The electric field of the phonon mode extends above the surface, coupling to semiconductor charges [239c597e947a7e]
- Strong coupling and hybridization between semiconductor charge and phonon mode [3bc9aef30dc3d1]
- Conversion efficiency further enhanced by semiconductor bias fields [b8c038a18ef16f]

**7. Piezoelectric Strain Actuation (Acoustoelastic Modulation)**
Taylor et al. (2021) demonstrated reconfigurable quantum phononic circuits via piezo-acoustomechanical interaction [Reconfigurable_quantum_phononic_circuits_via_piezo-acoustomechanical_interaction]. Key features:
- Piezoelectric strain actuation produces large phase velocity changes in AlN on suspended SiN [285f6dae7e3442]
- The acoustoelastic effect can reverse polarity and alter magnitude of frequency shift Δf [59586b08130f67]
- Bandstructure and group velocity of the guided mode mediate responsiveness to acoustomechanical effects [289e02833a5254]
- Increasing piezoelectric transducer overhang improves modulation [7b9e7879dc1da8]

**8. SQUID-Based Flux Tuning of SAW Resonators**
Andersson et al. (2020) demonstrated that SQUID impedance provides a means of flux tuning SAW resonators [Squeezing_and_Multimode_Entanglement_of_Surface_Acoustic_Wave_Phonons]. Key features:
- SQUID reflector couples more than 20 modes due to narrow free spectral range [45fb15da843176]
- Beam-splitting interaction can be implemented by a parametric drive [67c826b3bf9922]
- Exploiting multiple modes enables quantum simulation in synthetic dimensions [cf8914ce83a832]

**9. Additional Methods Mentioned in the Literature**
The introduction of the thermal modulation paper (Shao et al. 2022) provides a broader survey of tunable SAW methods, listing: mechanical nonlinear deformations, piezoelectrically-actuated deformation, electro-acoustic effects, spatiotemporal modulations, acoustoelectric coupling in semiconductors, magnetoelastic coupling, non-Hermitian physics, and circulating fluids [Thermal_Modulation_of_Gigahertz_Surface_Acoustic_Waves_on_Lithium_Niobate#4050]. The paper notes that the first three categories "still require high voltages to achieve a full π" phase shift, motivating the development of the lower-voltage thermal approach.

**Summary Comparison:**
- **Thermal**: largest phase shift per unit power, but slow (ms timescale, Hz bandwidth); phase-only in simple configuration
- **Electro-acoustic**: fast, works at mK, but requires higher voltages (53–135 V half-wave) and benefits from waveguide confinement
- **Quantum (SQUID)**: enables single-phonon-level control at mK, tunable coupling over 300:1 range
- **Adiabatic mode conversion**: passive, no external drive needed; converts between SAW modes for environmental robustness
- **PT-symmetric/nonlinear**: enables nonreciprocal (direction-dependent) transmission via circuit-tuned gain/loss
- **Electron-mediated nonlinearity**: enables frequency conversion (mixing) with orders-of-magnitude enhancement
- **Piezoelectric strain**: large frequency shifts via acoustoelastic effect, reconfigurable
- **SQUID flux tuning**: quantum-level control of resonator frequency and mode coupling

answer_raw:
Based on the scientific literature in this knowledge base, there are several distinct ways to modulate gigahertz surface acoustic waves (SAWs), spanning thermal, electrical, quantum, mechanical, and nonlinear approaches:

**1. Thermal Modulation (Thermo-Acoustic Modulation)**
Shao et al. (2022) demonstrated thermal modulation of GHz SAWs on lithium niobate (LN) substrates [Thermal_Modulation_of_Gigahertz_Surface_Acoustic_Waves_on_Lithium_Niobate]. The mechanism leverages the temperature dependence of LN's elastic constants to control the phase velocity of the acoustic wave [253879490f9f90]. Key results include:
- Phase changes exceeding 720° with only 2.6 dB of heater power on bulk LN, and >720° with 0.52 dB on LN-on-sapphire (LNSa) [24e2c027eafab6, cc1f5ef63ad0c3]
- 3-dB modulation bandwidths of 18 Hz (bulk LN) and 120 Hz (LNSa) [8deb32f6788410, e76c8b301bce66]
- Rise/fall times of 896/657 ms (bulk LN) and 313/212 ms (LNSa) [5f5b96ffce5b5e, 52411a7b555c03, f5c9a4704b0d57, 1f5f9544aae7aa]
- The modulation is phase-only: S21 amplitudes are unaffected by the heater [5908f01461466c]
- Thermo-acoustic modulators offer larger tuning range and require smaller voltages compared to electro-acoustic modulators [bfb62eaf05bd55]
- An acoustic Mach-Zehnder interferometer configuration enables amplitude modulation [70b6cd8f085b09]

**2. Electrical (Electro-Acoustic) Modulation**
Shao et al. (2021) demonstrated electrical control of SAWs via the electro-acoustic effect, where an applied electric field changes the elastic constants of the substrate [Electrical_Control_of_Surface_Acoustic_Waves]. Key features:
- The electro-acoustic effect is a parametric process valid at both room and millikelvin temperatures [ad7629f2454918]
- Confining the acoustic wave to a wavelength-scale waveguide (10 μm slot) with modulation electrodes enables strong modulation [a8123592fbdc8b, d8ccfc1c8fced5]
- Demonstrated phase and amplitude modulation, as well as an acoustic frequency shifter [0b771e85c233b0]
- Reconfigurable nonreciprocal modulation by tailoring phase matching [b75b8093ebfac7]
- Half-wave voltages of 53 V and 135 V; peak transmission at 2.532 GHz [3abe7acd990e54, 69accd53342cb2, b43c8c4cf40523]
- Propagation loss: 17 dB/cm at 300 K, 5 dB/cm at LN temperature, <1 dB/cm at 1.3 K [659602ecaa4606, 79fa00fc3fa8fd, 18fcb8f8b7c2f3]
- A key limitation: bulk components show small phase changes due to the weak electro-acoustic effect, motivating the waveguide confinement approach 
- Advantages over thermal: low-temperature compatibility and faster modulation speed [c3060f1eec396a]

**3. Quantum Control via Superconducting Qubits**
Satzinger et al. (2018) demonstrated quantum control of 4.0 GHz SAW phonons (wavelength 1 μm) at ~10 mK using a superconducting qubit coupled via a SQUID tunable coupler [Quantum_control_of_surface_acoustic-wave_phonons]. Key results:
- Coupling strength |g₀|/2π tunable from 2.3 ± 0.1 MHz up to 7.3 ± 0.1 MHz, a ratio of 300 [b9d421daaa7d4a, 489d60eebf93bf, f6ff310d8d9b92]
- Controllable generation of resonator Fock states [2643355475f23d]
- Adjusting g₀ away from zero shortens qubit lifetime (Purcell effect) [95a2b1bbab950a]

**4. Adiabatic Mode Conversion**
Wang et al. (2022) demonstrated adiabatic conversion between gigahertz quasi-Rayleigh and quasi-Love modes using a tapered phononic waveguide that exploits the anisotropic elastic properties of the substrate [Adiabatic_conversion_between_gigahertz_quasi-Rayleigh_and_quasi-Love_modes_for_p]. Key features:
- Nearly perfect mode conversion by adiabatically changing the wave number along the waveguide [321e7723365f1e]
- The quasi-Love mode has in-plane displacement, minimizing damping in air/liquid environments [8d7a2da85d0666]
- Conversion efficiency depends critically on adiabaticity (dw/dx must be small enough) [d7a1134eecd3a0]
- Mode coupling is mainly caused by the anisotropic substrate [9f72a5d58cd24e]

**5. Non-Reciprocal PT-Symmetric Modulation**
Shao et al. (2020) demonstrated nonreciprocal transmission of microwave acoustic waves in a nonlinear parity-time (PT)-symmetric system [Non-reciprocal_transmission_of_microwave_acoustic_waves_in_nonlinear_parity_time]. Key features:
- Leverages the strong piezoelectricity of LN to achieve fully tunable gain, loss, and nonlinearity of SAWs via an external circuit [f7fd6ea77b82d5]
- A negative-resistance circuit provides nonlinear gain with a tunable operating point [a55e5c1581484b]
- Saturation nonlinearity breaks time-reversal symmetry, enabling nonreciprocal transmission [cf8843d10b1d50]
- A 30-groove Bragg mirror provides stronger coupling, placing the system in the broken-PT regime [4c5a67aabcae83]

**6. Electron-Mediated Phononic Nonlinearity (Frequency Conversion)**
Hackett et al. (2024) demonstrated giant electron-mediated phononic nonlinearity in semiconductor-piezoelectric heterostructures [Giant_electron-mediated_phononic_nonlinearity_in_semiconductor_piezoelectric_het]. Key features:
- Phononic frequency conversion (sum-frequency and difference-frequency generation) enhanced by orders of magnitude via heterogeneous integration of high-mobility semiconductor films [880070cb5c7a09, 9306bfc2ad2d6c]
- The electric field of the phonon mode extends above the surface, coupling to semiconductor charges [239c597e947a7e]
- Strong coupling and hybridization between semiconductor charge and phonon mode [3bc9aef30dc3d1]
- Conversion efficiency further enhanced by semiconductor bias fields [b8c038a18ef16f]

**7. Piezoelectric Strain Actuation (Acoustoelastic Modulation)**
Taylor et al. (2021) demonstrated reconfigurable quantum phononic circuits via piezo-acoustomechanical interaction [Reconfigurable_quantum_phononic_circuits_via_piezo-acoustomechanical_interaction]. Key features:
- Piezoelectric strain actuation produces large phase velocity changes in AlN on suspended SiN [285f6dae7e3442]
- The acoustoelastic effect can reverse polarity and alter magnitude of frequency shift Δf [59586b08130f67]
- Bandstructure and group velocity of the guided mode mediate responsiveness to acoustomechanical effects [289e02833a5254]
- Increasing piezoelectric transducer overhang improves modulation [7b9e7879dc1da8]

**8. SQUID-Based Flux Tuning of SAW Resonators**
Andersson et al. (2020) demonstrated that SQUID impedance provides a means of flux tuning SAW resonators [Squeezing_and_Multimode_Entanglement_of_Surface_Acoustic_Wave_Phonons]. Key features:
- SQUID reflector couples more than 20 modes due to narrow free spectral range [45fb15da843176]
- Beam-splitting interaction can be implemented by a parametric drive [67c826b3bf9922]
- Exploiting multiple modes enables quantum simulation in synthetic dimensions [cf8914ce83a832]

**9. Additional Methods Mentioned in the Literature**
The introduction of the thermal modulation paper (Shao et al. 2022) provides a broader survey of tunable SAW methods, listing: mechanical nonlinear deformations, piezoelectrically-actuated deformation, electro-acoustic effects, spatiotemporal modulations, acoustoelectric coupling in semiconductors, magnetoelastic coupling, non-Hermitian physics, and circulating fluids [Thermal_Modulation_of_Gigahertz_Surface_Acoustic_Waves_on_Lithium_Niobate#4050]. The paper notes that the first three categories "still require high voltages to achieve a full π" phase shift, motivating the development of the lower-voltage thermal approach.

**Summary Comparison:**
- **Thermal**: largest phase shift per unit power, but slow (ms timescale, Hz bandwidth); phase-only in simple configuration
- **Electro-acoustic**: fast, works at mK, but requires higher voltages (53–135 V half-wave) and benefits from waveguide confinement
- **Quantum (SQUID)**: enables single-phonon-level control at mK, tunable coupling over 300:1 range
- **Adiabatic mode conversion**: passive, no external drive needed; converts between SAW modes for environmental robustness
- **PT-symmetric/nonlinear**: enables nonreciprocal (direction-dependent) transmission via circuit-tuned gain/loss
- **Electron-mediated nonlinearity**: enables frequency conversion (mixing) with orders-of-magnitude enhancement
- **Piezoelectric strain**: large frequency shifts via acoustoelastic effect, reconfigurable
- **SQUID flux tuning**: quantum-level control of resonator frequency and mode coupling

question: How can all-dielectri photonics crystal enhance fluorescence?
answer:
All-dielectric photonic crystals (PCs) enhance fluorescence through several distinct but often synergistic physical mechanisms. The literature in this knowledge base identifies the following principal channels:

**1. Purcell effect (spontaneous-emission rate enhancement)**
The most fundamental mechanism is the modification of the local density of optical states (LDOS) by the PC's electromagnetic band structure. Purcell's original prediction was that an atom placed in a wavelength-scale cavity radiates much faster than in free space . In a dielectric PC, the periodic modulation of refractive index redistributes the photonic density of states: at frequencies within a photonic bandgap the LDOS is strongly suppressed (even approaching zero), while at band edges or resonant defect modes it is enhanced . When a fluorophore's emission frequency coincides with an enhanced LDOS region, its spontaneous-emission rate increases, shortening the radiative lifetime and raising the quantum efficiency (QE) because the radiative channel outcompetes non-radiative decay . Because dielectric materials are lossless, the Purcell effect modifies QE without introducing additional non-radiative loss channels . The magnitude of the Purcell enhancement depends on the mode volume and quality factor of the resonant mode; thin-slab PCs may not always achieve the small mode volumes and high Q needed for very large Purcell factors because their resonances are often degenerate or leaky . The fluorescence lifetime in a PC has been shown to be a function of the crystal lattice parameter, in agreement with LDOS calculations .

**2. Light-extraction enhancement (Bragg scattering / zone folding)**
For 2-D thin-film PCs, the dominant enhancement mechanism is often not the Purcell effect but rather improved light extraction. The periodic structure acts as a 2-D diffraction grating: fluorescence that would normally be trapped as guided modes (total internal reflection) is Bragg-scattered into the escape cone of the collection optics . This "zone-folding" or Bragg-scattering mechanism redirects in-plane propagating photons into radiative channels, and for 2-D PCs the benefit from improved extraction typically far exceeds the Purcell contribution . The periodic patterned semiconductor film thus prevents light trapping . Angle-resolved photoluminescence from inside the PC provides a direct spectral readout of the internal 2-D band dispersion, confirming this extraction mechanism .

**3. Excitation enhancement (near-field and resonant coupling)**
The PC can also enhance the excitation rate of the fluorophore. When the excitation wavelength couples to leaky eigenmodes or guided-mode resonances of the PC, high-intensity near fields are formed at the surface, efficiently exciting nearby emitters . In the quantum-dot-on-PC-surface system, the overall enhancement is attributed to the combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering from leaky eigenmodes . Guided-mode resonances can channel internally generated light to the exterior under resonant coupling conditions .

**4. Heterostructure and multi-layer design strategies (simultaneous excitation and emission matching)**
A key design insight from the review literature is that the relative spectral position of the fluorescence excitation maximum, emission maximum, and the PC's optical resonances (stopband, bandgap, guided-mode resonances) substantially determines the nature and magnitude of enhancement . Homogeneous PCs with a single stopband can match either excitation or emission but not both. Heterostructure PCs overcome this:

- **Multiple Heterostructure Photonic Crystals (MHPC):** By stacking homogeneous crystals with different polystyrene-sphere sizes, a super-wide stopband is created that simultaneously overlaps both the excitation and emission spectra. The H-IV heterostructure sample achieved an additional 2.5-fold fluorescence enhancement relative to the best homogeneous 245 nm crystal because its widened bandgap matched both excitation and emission . The optical resonator environment formed by the stopband couples with the excitation light while periodic dielectric-constant modulation improves scattering . In contrast, in a homogeneous 245 nm PC only the emission light couples to the stopband, not the excitation . For homogeneous 160/200 nm crystals, the enhancement was mainly caused by a light-scattering mechanism . Reported enhancement factors for MHPC substrates range from 25-fold to more than 100-fold (on glass substrate), with a value of 102 at a specific concentration .

- **E-F-E double heterostructure (3D colloidal PCs):** The design uses an etalon configuration where two outer "E" (excitation-matching) layers reflect excitation light back into the central "F" (fluorescence-matching) layer, recycling the excitation to increase excitation efficiency . The F layer itself is a colloidal photonic crystal with a partial bandgap overlapping the fluorophore emission, acting as a strong resonator for the emitted light . This dual function—excitation recycling plus emission resonance—produces moderate-to-strong intensity enhancement . The modified emission lifetimes in these structures are a direct consequence of the photonic bandgap effects on the emission channel .

**5. Suppression of quenching (opal PCs)**
In addition to the optical mechanisms, opal-type all-dielectric PCs have been shown to effectively inhibit aggregation-promoted quenching of fluorophores, providing a chemical/physical protection benefit that further preserves fluorescence signal . The absence of a complete photonic bandgap in opaline crystals (due to their imperfect close-packing) means the enhancement is more moderate but still significant .

**6. Bandgap engineering and polarization considerations**
The PC bandgap can be interpreted as destructive interference of many reflections at high/low-index interfaces . Thin-slab PCs support a bandgap only for TE-polarized guided modes, which constrains the polarization of the enhanced emission . The PC's influence on LDOS and fluorophore lifetime is predominantly determined by the central position, bandwidth, and amplitude of the spectral feature (bandgap or resonance) relative to the emission line .

**Summary of the enhancement hierarchy:**
For 2-D thin-film dielectric PCs, light-extraction enhancement (Bragg scattering) is typically the dominant contribution, with the Purcell effect providing a secondary but important boost to quantum efficiency . For 3-D colloidal PCs and heterostructures, the design can simultaneously address excitation efficiency (via stopband matching or etalon recycling) and emission extraction (via bandgap/resonance coupling), yielding multiplicative enhancement factors that can exceed 100-fold in optimized configurations . The lossless dielectric nature of these structures ensures that the Purcell enhancement improves QE without adding non-radiative loss , distinguishing all-dielectric PCs from plasmonic alternatives.

answer_raw:
All-dielectric photonic crystals (PCs) enhance fluorescence through several distinct but often synergistic physical mechanisms. The literature in this knowledge base identifies the following principal channels:

**1. Purcell effect (spontaneous-emission rate enhancement)**
The most fundamental mechanism is the modification of the local density of optical states (LDOS) by the PC's electromagnetic band structure. Purcell's original prediction was that an atom placed in a wavelength-scale cavity radiates much faster than in free space [43acbc0d49e3be]. In a dielectric PC, the periodic modulation of refractive index redistributes the photonic density of states: at frequencies within a photonic bandgap the LDOS is strongly suppressed (even approaching zero), while at band edges or resonant defect modes it is enhanced [ec198f968e2ccc, f83cc397f4da41]. When a fluorophore's emission frequency coincides with an enhanced LDOS region, its spontaneous-emission rate increases, shortening the radiative lifetime and raising the quantum efficiency (QE) because the radiative channel outcompetes non-radiative decay [651eef8bafbd10, 4364e8f411e5d5, 0fe5cc6fd2e25d]. Because dielectric materials are lossless, the Purcell effect modifies QE without introducing additional non-radiative loss channels [0fe5cc6fd2e25d]. The magnitude of the Purcell enhancement depends on the mode volume and quality factor of the resonant mode; thin-slab PCs may not always achieve the small mode volumes and high Q needed for very large Purcell factors because their resonances are often degenerate or leaky [5fd2c67e853462]. The fluorescence lifetime in a PC has been shown to be a function of the crystal lattice parameter, in agreement with LDOS calculations [41c5a5f0145652].

**2. Light-extraction enhancement (Bragg scattering / zone folding)**
For 2-D thin-film PCs, the dominant enhancement mechanism is often not the Purcell effect but rather improved light extraction. The periodic structure acts as a 2-D diffraction grating: fluorescence that would normally be trapped as guided modes (total internal reflection) is Bragg-scattered into the escape cone of the collection optics [baaab8088da62e, 2b57ed726dfce2, 27ba319cc08f5e]. This "zone-folding" or Bragg-scattering mechanism redirects in-plane propagating photons into radiative channels, and for 2-D PCs the benefit from improved extraction typically far exceeds the Purcell contribution [2b57ed726dfce2]. The periodic patterned semiconductor film thus prevents light trapping [27ba319cc08f5e]. Angle-resolved photoluminescence from inside the PC provides a direct spectral readout of the internal 2-D band dispersion, confirming this extraction mechanism [a812b7168b0d79].

**3. Excitation enhancement (near-field and resonant coupling)**
The PC can also enhance the excitation rate of the fluorophore. When the excitation wavelength couples to leaky eigenmodes or guided-mode resonances of the PC, high-intensity near fields are formed at the surface, efficiently exciting nearby emitters [802c0244088f75, 70869a665dd761]. In the quantum-dot-on-PC-surface system, the overall enhancement is attributed to the combination of high-intensity near fields and strong coherent scattering from leaky eigenmodes [802c0244088f75]. Guided-mode resonances can channel internally generated light to the exterior under resonant coupling conditions [7955899e869348, 4fdbe5e019d4af].

**4. Heterostructure and multi-layer design strategies (simultaneous excitation and emission matching)**
A key design insight from the review literature is that the relative spectral position of the fluorescence excitation maximum, emission maximum, and the PC's optical resonances (stopband, bandgap, guided-mode resonances) substantially determines the nature and magnitude of enhancement [fe7901f10cbe05]. Homogeneous PCs with a single stopband can match either excitation or emission but not both. Heterostructure PCs overcome this:

- **Multiple Heterostructure Photonic Crystals (MHPC):** By stacking homogeneous crystals with different polystyrene-sphere sizes, a super-wide stopband is created that simultaneously overlaps both the excitation and emission spectra. The H-IV heterostructure sample achieved an additional 2.5-fold fluorescence enhancement relative to the best homogeneous 245 nm crystal because its widened bandgap matched both excitation and emission [f3b103cf33d874, aa3928d34e8339]. The optical resonator environment formed by the stopband couples with the excitation light while periodic dielectric-constant modulation improves scattering [0a4271f39cc0dd]. In contrast, in a homogeneous 245 nm PC only the emission light couples to the stopband, not the excitation [676fc67e0f4d4c]. For homogeneous 160/200 nm crystals, the enhancement was mainly caused by a light-scattering mechanism [35c3392385cee8]. Reported enhancement factors for MHPC substrates range from 25-fold to more than 100-fold (on glass substrate), with a value of 102 at a specific concentration [8b73b8c1bc5a6b, ae8f949a772726, 1e6298f80df784, 5fd063d26cf6e5, d2af2671c00736].

- **E-F-E double heterostructure (3D colloidal PCs):** The design uses an etalon configuration where two outer "E" (excitation-matching) layers reflect excitation light back into the central "F" (fluorescence-matching) layer, recycling the excitation to increase excitation efficiency [3ba63537117f53, 1590e77a3393ae]. The F layer itself is a colloidal photonic crystal with a partial bandgap overlapping the fluorophore emission, acting as a strong resonator for the emitted light [fc35116c39b1ea]. This dual function—excitation recycling plus emission resonance—produces moderate-to-strong intensity enhancement [792ad064cb4423]. The modified emission lifetimes in these structures are a direct consequence of the photonic bandgap effects on the emission channel [44ef8c6219062c].

**5. Suppression of quenching (opal PCs)**
In addition to the optical mechanisms, opal-type all-dielectric PCs have been shown to effectively inhibit aggregation-promoted quenching of fluorophores, providing a chemical/physical protection benefit that further preserves fluorescence signal [b98828304af77b]. The absence of a complete photonic bandgap in opaline crystals (due to their imperfect close-packing) means the enhancement is more moderate but still significant [d220a76dea909c].

**6. Bandgap engineering and polarization considerations**
The PC bandgap can be interpreted as destructive interference of many reflections at high/low-index interfaces [715d383b1f5dba]. Thin-slab PCs support a bandgap only for TE-polarized guided modes, which constrains the polarization of the enhanced emission [9fe4235abdfb2b]. The PC's influence on LDOS and fluorophore lifetime is predominantly determined by the central position, bandwidth, and amplitude of the spectral feature (bandgap or resonance) relative to the emission line [8b900f875c3cc9].

**Summary of the enhancement hierarchy:**
For 2-D thin-film dielectric PCs, light-extraction enhancement (Bragg scattering) is typically the dominant contribution, with the Purcell effect providing a secondary but important boost to quantum efficiency [2b57ed726dfce2, baaab8088da62e]. For 3-D colloidal PCs and heterostructures, the design can simultaneously address excitation efficiency (via stopband matching or etalon recycling) and emission extraction (via bandgap/resonance coupling), yielding multiplicative enhancement factors that can exceed 100-fold in optimized configurations [f3b103cf33d874, 5fd063d26cf6e5]. The lossless dielectric nature of these structures ensures that the Purcell enhancement improves QE without adding non-radiative loss [0fe5cc6fd2e25d], distinguishing all-dielectric PCs from plasmonic alternatives.

question: How does particle binding to a high-Q optical microcavity induce a resonance shift, and what are the limitations and enhancements required for sensitive single-protein detection using cavity optomechanics?
answer:
**Mechanism of Resonance Shift**

The fundamental mechanism by which particle binding induces a resonance shift in high-Q optical microcavities relies on the interaction between the bound particle and the cavity's evanescent field. In whispering gallery mode (WGM) resonators, such as silica microspheres or microtoroids, the optical mode is confined to a small volume, and the evanescent field extends into the surrounding medium, shifting the resonance frequency upon interaction with adsorbed particles . The magnitude of this shift is governed by the spatial overlap between the particle and the optical mode, characterized by the evanescent field extension length $L$. For a silica microsphere with a diameter of $450 \pm 10 \mu m$ , the evanescent field extension is approximately $L \sim 50$ nm at a wavelength of 633 nm [d428718c05c1d8] and increases to $L \sim 80$ nm at 1060 nm [9244030df7ca12]. The high quality factors of these cavities, such as $Q \sim 3 \times 10^6$ at 633 nm [3e3574de33bc86] and $Q \sim 5 \times 10^6$ at 1060 nm [8e937c39132008], ensure that even minute perturbations to the effective refractive index result in measurable wavelength shifts. In the specific case of nanoparticle-based protein detection, the binding of a protein, modeled as a sphere with a radius of 3.4 nm and a refractive index of 1.45 [7887d6e9fe0538][dd344d23d8bb2e], perturbs the local dielectric environment. While the generalized Mie theory is used to model the WGM-NP sensor [2df2df3fa494db], the direct adsorption of a single BSA molecule at the center of the evanescent field does not produce a detectable shift in the standard configuration . This limitation arises because the volume of a single protein is too small relative to the mode volume to induce a sufficient change in the effective index for detection at the current noise floor.

**Limitations for Single-Protein Detection**

The primary limitation for sensitive single-protein detection using standard cavity optomechanics is the insufficient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for single-molecule events. As noted, the adsorption of a single BSA molecule does not yield a detectable resonance shift . Detectable shifts are only observed when the BSA concentration is higher than 1 $\mu M$, where an additional increase in the shift signal is observed . This indicates that the current sensitivity is limited to ensemble measurements rather than single-molecule resolution. Furthermore, mechanical stability poses a significant challenge; WGM biosensors utilizing fiber couplers suffer from mechanical vibrations of the fiber taper, which can obscure small resonance shifts [b7c4a1ae165259]. In the context of cavity optomechanics, the mechanical frequency shift induced by radiation pressure is dependent on the pump detuning and the mechanical frequency $\Omega_m$. A mechanical frequency shift occurs when $\Omega_m > 1/2 \cdot \kappa$ and the pump detuning is small [a9e6ec9e3474d9]. However, there exists a specific pump detuning where the radiation-pressure induced mechanical frequency shift is zero, even though damping or amplification is non-zero [e42f5db180f299]. This null point in the frequency shift response limits the ability to use mechanical frequency shifts as a direct probe for particle binding unless the operating point is carefully chosen. Additionally, at high intensities, a plateau in the response beyond 1 MHz to 200 MHz is attributed to the Kerr effect (intensity-dependent refractive index) of fused silica, which can saturate the sensor response [58501071a0ed08].

**Enhancements for Sensitive Detection**

To overcome the limitations of single-protein detection, several enhancement strategies have been developed, focusing on plasmonic coupling, exceptional point (EP) physics, and on-chip optomechanical integration.

*Plasmonic Enhancement:*
Introducing receptor-linked plasmonic nanoparticles (NPs) onto the microsphere circumference amplifies the resonance wavelength shift by orders of magnitude [7595eb798c7693]. This is achieved through the formation of hybrid photonic-plasmonic modes, which feature significant electric field enhancement on the NP surface [e5058469308bac]. Calculations indicate that the coupling of WGM to the NP plasmon resonance can result in up to a 3 orders-of-magnitude increase in electric field intensity on the NP surface [1734f951cd7075]. This plasmonic field enhancement leads to a demonstrated gain in sensitivity of plasmon-enhanced WGM over non-plasmonic WGM biosensors [1c53891f52e692]. The hybrid modes also exhibit orders-of-magnitude larger Q-factors in the WGM-NP structure [16dc7d4a068f41], and the coupling enhances the signal-to-noise ratio [f861b894bec60c]. However, strong WGM coupling to the NP collective electron oscillations near the NP dipole LSP resonance can decrease the Q-factors of hybrid modes in the 520-580 nm range [9ce982aff029ce], representing a trade-off between field enhancement and cavity quality. In a related "antenna-in-nanocavity" configuration, photons are trapped in an ultrasmall mode volume for a time five orders of magnitude longer than a single pass ($Q\lambda/L_{eff} \sim 10^5$), significantly enhancing the reactive back action of molecules to trapped photons [95eb8838490445].

*Exceptional Point (EP) Sensing:*
Operating the microcavity at an exceptional point (EP) offers a distinct enhancement in sensitivity. The EP sensor exhibits a larger frequency split than a diabolic point (DP) sensor for the same nanoparticles [ff1d4c0bbe388b]. The sensitivity is enhanced when operating at the EP, with a demonstrated more than threefold enhancement in frequency splitting detection [ac8e1f7fa19470]. Specifically, for a 1-$\mu m$ SiO$_2$ sphere, the frequency splitting $|\Delta\Omega|$ is enhanced by a factor of 3 to 3.5 compared to $|\Delta\Omega_{DP}|$ [d1d0002091debb]. This enhancement is valid when the square root term in the relevant equation is real, ensuring the frequency splitting at the EP is larger than at the DP [686340c5b37f31]. The EP sensor's response is independent of the azimuthal position of the particle [7ecd63996df856]. However, a significant limitation of EP operation is that individual linewidths increase to approximately 7 times the frequency splitting . To resolve this splitting when linewidths are large, the use of a microlaser (optical gain) is recommended [a7994805c7bc0f]. The target particle drives the system slightly away from the EP, introducing a standing-wave component [644747daa4572f]. In a specific demonstration, the imaginary part of the refractive index was measured as $-Im n = 0.00043$ [4256b090474bb7].

*On-Chip Optomechanical Integration:*
On-chip optomechanical systems provide high sensitivity through precise control of coupling and noise floors. These systems demonstrate an angular noise floor of 4 nrad/$\sqrt{Hz}$ [f8322a51a32c86], a displacement noise floor of 2 fm/$\sqrt{Hz}$ [0a768f3024fbcf], a force sensitivity of 132 aN/$\sqrt{Hz}$ [0056e6d9a10b1f], and a torque sensitivity of $4 \times 10^{-20}$ N·m/$\sqrt{Hz}$ [4ec582f2a1c15e]. The resonant enhancement in these systems scales with the optical Q factor, increasing the slope of the response [af9eeb7e3506c3]. To further improve performance, operating in a vacuum drastically reduces damping, thereby increasing the mechanical Q factor [779cb70f487b6c]. Additionally, using materials with a high index of refraction enhances the mechanical resonator's perturbation of the optical cavity [de75a73e5e4502]. The optomechanical coupling is controlled by the gap between the mechanical and optical resonators [efbb89bd83789e]. In a specific high-sensitivity nanoparticle detection experiment, a shift of $0.4 \pm 0.2$ fm for 12.5-nm beads was observable at 11 seconds with an SNR of 2, with the step amplitude enhanced by measuring on a longer-wavelength resonance [33de6090aee09c].

In summary, while standard WGM cavities lack the sensitivity for single-protein detection due to small mode volume interactions and mechanical noise [b7c4a1ae165259], enhancements through plasmonic field concentration [7595eb798c7693][1734f951cd7075], exceptional point physics [ac8e1f7fa19470][d1d0002091debb], and optimized on-chip optomechanical designs [f8322a51a32c86][0a768f3024fbcf] provide the necessary sensitivity improvements for detecting minute biological perturbations.
