answer_raw:
The successful preparation of quantum states of phonons has been demonstrated across a variety of mechanical systems, ranging from nanomechanical resonators and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices to macroscopic mechanical oscillators. The prepared states include the quantum ground state, specific Fock states (number states), superposition states, squeezed states, entangled states, and Schrödinger cat states.

**Ground State Preparation**
The quantum ground state of a mechanical mode has been successfully prepared in multiple platforms. O'Connell et al. (2010) demonstrated the cooling of a 3.68 GHz nanomechanical mode into its quantum mechanical ground state, achieving a phonon occupancy of 0.85±0.04 [019c76a6b56b4b, 459c50b7e0841d]. In a separate experiment, Wollack et al. (2021) prepared the ground state of a 3.68 GHz mode with a state fidelity of 0.913±0.003, utilizing a dispersive cooperativity of C=490 [6f181c7dd592a9, 07394644362872]. Additionally, Kotler et al. (2020) prepared a fiducial cold state via ground-state cooling, characterized by a diagonal covariance matrix, which served as the basis for subsequent entanglement experiments .

**Fock States (Number States)**
The preparation of specific phonon Fock states has been achieved in both SAW and bulk acoustic-wave resonators. Satzinger et al. (2018) controllably generated resonator states in a 4.0 GHz SAW system at 10 mK using a transmon qubit [2643355475f23d]. The resulting state populations were measured as 47.3% for the |2> state, 38.2% for the |1> state, and 14.5% for the |0> state [019c76a6b56b4b, 27b52bcb2cc8bc, be6457d450838c]. Chu et al. (2018) prepared Fock states in a bulk acoustic-wave resonator, with populations agreeing well with expected Poisson distributions [2012ff98d59882]. Specifically, Wigner tomography was performed on nominally prepared states |1>, (|0>+|1>)/√2, and |2> [Creation_and_control_of_multi-phonon_Fock_states_in_a_bulk_acoustic-wave_resonat#16200]. The quantum nature of these states was highlighted by the negativity of the Wigner functions [c4de296b99d66b, b11240aeb45af5]. Wollack et al. (2021) also demonstrated the preparation of the |1> state, with negative values in the Wigner function confirming its quantum nature [cce093779c1c66]. The tomography protocol for these states agreed with quantum master equation simulations including decoherences [4a799a5703b85f].

**Superposition and Cat States**
Schrödinger cat states, defined as coherent superpositions of two or more states with well-separated phase space distributions, have been prepared in macroscopic mechanical systems. Bild et al. (2022) prepared cat states in a 16-microgram mechanical oscillator coupled to a transmon qubit [6f62c0784bf8c1, Schr_dinger_cat_states_of_a_16-microgram_mechanical_oscillator#4050]. This system, with a mass on the order of 30 nanograms, represents the most massive object in a cat state to date [4cdadf8cfedd2c]. The negative Wigner features of these states were observed to disappear on a time scale much faster than the energy relaxation time T1, with faster decaying negativity observed for larger cat states [15f62c0784bf8c1, 17f62c0784bf8c1]. Additionally, Chu et al. (2018) prepared the superposition state (|0>+|1>)/√2 in a bulk acoustic-wave resonator [Creation_and_control_of_multi-phonon_Fock_states_in_a_bulk_acoustic-wave_resonat#16200].

**Squeezed and Entangled States**
Non-classical states such as squeezed and entangled phonon states have also been successfully generated. Andersson et al. (2020) demonstrated two-mode squeezing of SAW phonons and four-mode multipartite entanglement in a multimode SAW resonator with a SQUID-integrated Bragg reflector . Two-mode squeezed states were generated between phonons in different SAW modes using a parametric drive, with squeezing observed below the pump-off level in all four mode pairs [60616538e6fc24, d50b90c497f10a]. Extending the pump scheme to four tones demonstrated multipartite entanglement [73e3e90bbfacb3].

Entanglement between mechanical oscillators has been achieved in both remote and local configurations. Riedinger et al. (2017) observed entanglement between two remote mechanical oscillators with >99.8% confidence [0944a4d18d5d25]. Kotler et al. (2020) deterministically entangled two mechanical drumheads (70 pg) using pulsed electromechanics, demonstrating a clear signature of drum-drum interaction through the correlation of x1, x2 and anticorrelation of p1, p2 [58ef74224232d0, f112dc383e47dc]. Bienfait et al. (2020) demonstrated two-phonon entanglement using an acoustic Fabry-Perot interferometer in a quantum eraser protocol, opening the door to two-phonon interferometry [99bad2a6c05fbb, 225d324d5370dc].

**Heralded and Non-Classical States**
Jiang et al. (2023) demonstrated the optically heralded addition of microwave photons, a process that generates non-classical states. The experiment achieved a heralding rate of 15 Hz and an efficiency of ~35% [0f3202de6b2057, b6f17a051706dd]. The optical-to-microwave conversion added noise was n_added,μo = 99±10, and the thermal noise was less than two [53Optically_heralded_microwave_photon_addition#16200, 24985647ca9fbd]. The violation of the Cauchy-Schwarz bound and the conditional g^(2) inequality constituted an unambiguous demonstration of non-classicality [11e8f043ca21c0].

**Limitations and Gaps**
While individual phonon-number states |0> and |1> have been resolved in gigahertz systems, Lee et al. (2023) state that the resolution of individual phonon-number states such as |0> and |1> has not yet been demonstrated for subgigahertz mechanical systems, despite achieving a qubit-phonon coupling rate g ≈ 2π×14 MHz [340b2e04b8f0edc7, 33a2dd30091c8b7d]. The consulted records did not surface specific details on the preparation of coherent states or thermal states as distinct, targeted quantum state preparations, nor did they provide data on Fock states beyond |2> in the context of the cited experimental demonstrations.

Developing effective personalized systems to improve the understanding of scientific concepts and jargon across diverse domains and expertise levels requires a multi-faceted approach that integrates advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), domain-specific adaptation techniques, and curriculum-based learning strategies. The consulted records indicate that no single method suffices; rather, effectiveness is achieved by balancing knowledge injection, computational efficiency, and the mitigation of catastrophic forgetting while tailoring outputs to specific user needs.

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Knowledge Injection**
A primary strategy for enhancing scientific understanding is the integration of RAG pipelines, which allow Large Language Models (LLMs) to access up-to-date and domain-specific information without requiring the model to memorize all facts. In an agricultural case study evaluating Llama2-13B, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, the implementation of a RAG pipeline significantly improved performance metrics . Specifically, the Recall metric increased from 61.9% to 87.8% when fine-tuning was applied to the RAG pipeline , and Recall@top-3 improved from 75.0% to 81.5% . These results suggest that combining retrieval with fine-tuning is more effective than retrieval alone for domain-specific tasks. However, the goal of knowledge injection in such systems is not necessarily to teach the model new knowledge, but rather to enable it to access and utilize existing information effectively . This is particularly relevant in niche domains where the volume of specific jargon is vast. Furthermore, RAG has the potential to address challenges in medicine by providing LLMs with relevant documents retrieved from up-to-date sources, thereby improving the accuracy of scientific explanations .

**Domain Adaptation and Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting**
To handle scientific jargon across different domains, systems must adapt to specific linguistic and conceptual structures without losing general capabilities. Directly tuning Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) on domain-specific corpora using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses previously acquired knowledge . To address this, the MixDA (Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters) framework decouples Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) into original pre-trained FFNs, which retain old-domain knowledge, and novel domain adapters . The paper states that a mixture-of-adapters gate dynamically fuses knowledge from different domain adapters, allowing the system to switch between domains effectively . This approach utilizes a two-stage adapter-tuning process: first, a domain-specific adapter is trained on unlabeled data, and second, a task-specific adapter is trained on labeled data . Since knowledge is stored in FFNs, this plug-in approach is effective in mitigating catastrophic forgetting while enabling domain-specific adaptation .

Alternatively, the REPLUG method treats the LM as a black box and tunes the retriever instead of the model itself . This approach improved the performance of the GPT-3 175B LM by 6.3%  and increased the 5-shot MMLU score for Codex by 5.1% . In STEM domains, REPLUG LSR outperformed the original method by 1.9% . Additionally, REPLUG demonstrated a 9.0% gain in GPT-2 Small BPB, reducing it from 1.33 to 1.21 . Other methods, such as Just CHOP (LayerChop), require no domain-specific data selection, offering a simpler path to adaptation . Knowledge Inheritance (KI) has also been shown to be more training-efficient than self-learning for domain adaptation, such as when adapting RoBERTa to Computer Science and Biology domains .

**Personalization and Expertise-Level Adaptation**
Personalizing systems for different expertise levels involves controlling the model's behavior to match the user's needs. Self-RAG trains a single arbitrary LM to adaptively retrieve passages on-demand and generate reflections on both retrieved passages and its own generations using special tokens . The paper states that these reflection tokens make the LM controllable during inference, enabling it to tailor its behavior to diverse task requirements . This controllability is crucial for adjusting the depth of explanation based on the user's expertise. Furthermore, Self-RAG provides citations for each segment with self-assessment, which helps users verify factual errors . The critic model in this framework is supervised on a dataset of inputs, outputs, and correctness labels, ensuring that the model can evaluate its own reliability .

For local, user-tailored models where data privacy is a concern, the intersection of Federated Learning (FL) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is relevant . The MoErging survey notes that zero-shot MoErging methods rely on the generalization capabilities of pre-trained expert models and the routing mechanism . However, embedding-based routers may falter in highly specialized domains, suggesting that routing strategies must be carefully selected . The survey highlights trade-offs in routing frequency (adaptability vs. computational efficiency vs. consistency) and expert selection (efficiency vs. routing accuracy vs. knowledge aggregation) . Classifier-based routing is best for data-rich complex routing, while task-specific routing is ideal for production environments, though it should be avoided when broad generalization is needed . Router-free methods are well-suited to certain applications . Additionally, the PEL-MoE method customizes MoE models by adapting a global model from a server and fine-tuning a local expert model with a local router, a technique restated from another paper .

**Curriculum Learning and Data Quality**
Effective personalization also depends on the quality and sequencing of training data. Curriculum learning involves multiple training stages to gradually increase the complexity of the data . One approach maps data quality into a 2D space based on image-text correlation and model perplexity to select data for these stages . This 2D space is used to construct multi-stage subsets of varying quality, allowing the model to learn from simpler concepts before tackling complex scientific jargon . The Skill-it framework demonstrates that curriculum learning can be performed at the group level, exploring various pacing functions and mixing rates to optimize learning [Chen#59400]. Adding curated high-quality cross-domain data is proposed as a key path for improving model architecture and understanding .

**Challenges in Multilingual and Cross-Domain Understanding**
Understanding scientific concepts across different languages and domains remains challenging. The MKQA benchmark, which includes 10k QA pairs across 26 languages, shows that the best English F1 score is only 52.3% . The task is particularly challenging in low-resource languages . Analysis of MKQA answers reveals that 42.2% are predominantly entities or atomic, while 32.4% are unanswerable or long . Despite these challenges, query translation acceptance rates can be high, with one metric showing 92.24% , and answer acceptance rates reaching 89.32% and 97.03% in different contexts . These statistics highlight the variability in system performance across different aspects of multilingual scientific QA.

**Design Principles and Ethical Considerations**
Designing these systems requires attention to ethical and educational implications. The DExperts paper recommends that future work should develop systems for mitigating harmful language that can be personalized to users' diverse needs . In the context of ethical xenotransplantation, the paper states that spurious concerns are ameliorated when public understanding of science improves and scientific understanding of ethics increases, highlighting a desperate need for better education of both the public and scientists . Furthermore, emerging technologies like 3D printing for medical phantoms have great potential for personalized medicine, suggesting that technical advancements in one domain can inform personalized educational tools in another . The EPR effect notes that nanoparticles could be personalized according to a patient's disease state, a concept restated from another paper that underscores the broader trend of personalization in scientific applications .

**Computational Efficiency and Test-Time Scaling**
Finally, the efficiency of these systems is critical for widespread deployment. Scaling LLM test-time compute by selecting the best search setting for a given question difficulty and compute budget can nearly outperform best-of-N methods using up to 4x less compute . These methods are applicable to other scaling approaches, offering a path to more efficient personalized systems . Few-shot recalibration enables the identification of domain-specific confidence thresholds, which can be used to adjust the system's output based on the user's expertise level . Additionally, improving text embeddings allows models to effectively perform personalized passkey retrieval, further enhancing the ability to tailor information to specific users .

The consulted records did not surface specific details on how to explicitly map expertise levels (e.g., novice vs. expert) to specific system parameters beyond the general controllability offered by reflection tokens in Self-RAG and the confidence thresholds in few-shot recalibration. Similarly, while cross-domain jargon handling is addressed through domain adapters and RAG, specific linguistic strategies for jargon simplification were not detailed in the provided notes.

The EPR effect notes that nanoparticles could be personalized according to a patient's disease state, a concept restated from another paper that underscores the broader trend of personalization in scientific applications [bbef655501dbac].

**Computational Efficiency and Test-Time Scaling**
Finally, the efficiency of these systems is critical for widespread deployment. Scaling LLM test-time compute by selecting the best search setting for a given question difficulty and compute budget can nearly outperform best-of-N methods using up to 4x less compute [15868bf0c54c3d]. These methods are applicable to other scaling approaches, offering a path to more efficient personalized systems [62bdcf659bfa27]. Few-shot recalibration enables the identification of domain-specific confidence thresholds, which can be used to adjust the system's output based on the user's expertise level [d98672b86a73cd]. Additionally, improving text embeddings allows models to effectively perform personalized passkey retrieval, further enhancing the ability to tailor information to specific users [2bfc6458362691].

The consulted records did not surface specific details on how to explicitly map expertise levels (e.g., novice vs. expert) to specific system parameters beyond the general controllability offered by reflection tokens in Self-RAG and the confidence thresholds in few-shot recalibration. Similarly, while cross-domain jargon handling is addressed through domain adapters and RAG, specific linguistic strategies for jargon simplification were not detailed in the provided notes.

question: What are the recent research advancements in enhancing fluorescence for imaging?
answer:
Recent research on enhancing fluorescence for imaging has advanced along several complementary axes: photonic-crystal (PC) substrates that reshape the local density of optical states, plasmonic nanoantennas that concentrate fields at the nanoscale, hybrid photonic–plasmonic and cavity-coupled architectures, and improved fluorescent probes (notably quantum dots). The corpus below synthesizes the principal mechanisms, quantitative gains, and application-level implications reported across these lines of work.

**1. Photonic-crystal-enhanced fluorescence (PCCE) — the dominant platform**

The central idea is to engineer a periodic dielectric structure whose bandgap or guided-mode resonances overlap with the excitation and/or emission wavelengths of the fluorophore, thereby (a) increasing the local excitation field, (b) modifying the radiative decay rate (Purcell effect), and (c) redirecting emitted photons into the collection cone. The review by Xiong et al. (2023) frames the field: only <30% of emitted light is typically detected even with sophisticated optical set-ups , and the relative position of the excitation/emission maxima with respect to the PC's optical resonances "substantially influences" the nature and magnitude of enhancement . The review also notes a field-wide shift toward lossless dielectric platforms over metal plasmonics because of high energy dissipation in metals , and identifies the urgent need for sensor substrates that simultaneously enhance excitation, extraction, and quantum efficiency .

*2D photonic crystals (photonic slabs).* A 2D PC produced a 3000-fold signal enhancement in a single-molecule detection context . In a separate study, quantum dots (QDs) on a 2D PC (period 300 nm, TiO₂ thickness 125 nm) showed a resonant fluorescence enhancement of 108.89 ± 4.09× versus an unpatterned surface, with a non-resonant control at 13.21 ± 0.26× and a near-field-only contribution of 8.24 ± 0.36× . The mechanism was attributed to the combination of high-intensity near fields and Bragg scattering of coupled radiation out of the structure . A key design insight from this work is the "doubly resonant" scheme: the PC is engineered so that leaky eigenmodes exist at both the absorption and emission wavelengths, so that external excitation of the leaky modes forms high-intensity near fields that efficiently excite the QDs, while coupling of the fluorescence to overlapping leaky modes plus Bragg scattering greatly reduces reabsorption . A low Q-factor (~92) of the extraction modes was found beneficial because it allows the coupled radiation to be scattered out rather than trapped . The authors explicitly state that this doubly resonant scheme for enhancing QD emission had not been demonstrated before their report .

*PC coupled to an optical cavity.* Pokhriyal et al. (2013) demonstrated that coupling a 2D PC to an underlying Fabry–Perot cavity produces even higher evanescent fields on the PC surface than the PC alone . The coupled mode repeats every ~220 nm cavity length (≈λ_eff/2, constructive interference), and without the PC the structure behaves as a weak FP cavity without strong evanescent fields . The underlying cavity coupled to the PC resonance increases the evanescent field intensity on the PC surface . The review cites a 360-fold enhancement achieved by coupling a PC leaky mode to an underlying Fabry–Perot cavity through a gold mirror .

*Leaky-mode-assisted extraction.* Ganesh et al. (2008) showed that the PC approach relies on coupling trapped light to free space via leaky modes created by the periodic structuring . Controlling the leaky-mode dispersion by tailoring PC properties redirects emitted light into preferred directions, enhancing collection efficiency . The enhancement mechanism is resonant redirection of emitted radiation .

*3D colloidal photonic crystals (CPhCs) and heterostructures.* Eftekhari et al. (2015) reported "anomalous" fluorescence enhancement from double heterostructure 3D colloidal PCs. The E-F-E (excitation–fluorescence–excitation) configuration acts as an etalon: two E layers reflect excitation light into the F layer, recycling it to increase excitation efficiency . The F layer is a CPhC with a partial bandgap overlapping the emission wavelength, acting as a strong resonator . The two E layers additionally form an optical resonator for the excitation light . For Rhodamine B, the E-F-E structure achieved an additional 5-fold enhancement over monolithic E CPhCs , a 4.3-fold acceleration of emission dynamics , and a ~6× improvement over monolithic CPhCs , reaching thousand-fold enhancement compared to a reference . The review cites a 320-fold luminescence enhancement of [Ru(dpp)₃] on 3D opal PCs  and a 60-fold increase for Cy-5-conjugated streptavidin on a 1D PC .

*Multi-heterostructure colloidal PCs (MHPCs).* Zhang et al. (2018) introduced a "universal" fluorescence enhancement substrate based on multiple heterostructure PCs. The H-IV sample, formed by stacking homogeneous crystals with different polystyrene sphere sizes, exhibited a super-wide stopband from 280 to 650 nm , enabling simultaneous matching of excitation and emission wavelengths . This yielded an additional 2.5-fold fluorescence enhancement over a homogeneous 245 nm film . The mechanism involves an optical resonator environment from the stopband that couples with excitation light and scattering, improved via periodic dielectric constant modulation . In contrast, homogeneous 160/200 nm crystals showed enhancement mainly from light scattering , and the H-I sample did not display obvious bandgap broadening . The MHPC platform was demonstrated as a fluorescence sensing enhancement platform for Cr(VI) detection  and described as having "extraordinary ability to enhance FL signal for most commonly used fluorescent media" .

*Purcell effect and lifetime modification.* Photonic crystals modify the radiative lifetime of emitters via redistribution of the photonic density of states . A dielectric PC produces quantum efficiency enhancement through the Purcell effect . PC resonant modes provide photonic dispersion that controls the angular distribution of emitted photons .

**2. Plasmonic nanoantennas and hybrid photonic–plasmonic systems**

Plasmonic nanoantennas (e.g., gold bowtie antennas) create highly enhanced local electromagnetic fields when pumped resonantly . Kinkhabwala et al. (2009) demonstrated that bowtie antennas with smaller gaps (below 40 nm) produce higher local field strengths than larger-gap bowties and single triangles , and that the local field enhancement is highly dependent on the bowtie gap size . A key finding is that low-quantum-efficiency emitters have much higher potential fluorescence brightness enhancements than high-QE emitters when placed on plasmonic nanoantennas . Deep sub-wavelength confinement in these structures achieves a near-unity emission coupling factor despite the 2D isotropic nature of the emitters .

Hybrid photonic–plasmonic systems combine the field concentration of plasmonics with the low-loss guidance of photonics. A hybrid photonic coupling between nanoparticles and an underlying PC enhances fluorescence . The review notes that PCCE and PCEF (plasmonic fluorescence enhancement) platforms substantially differ in structural design and photonic response , and that novel nano-engineering methodologies combining both platforms can achieve further enhancement .

**3. Enhanced emission and low-threshold lasing**

Zhen et al. (2013) demonstrated that optical resonances (exceptional points in non-Hermitian systems) modify light–matter interaction by enhancing absorption via pump coupling and improving extraction . The emission enhancement arises from two mechanisms: local excitation field enhancement and extraction rate enhancement . Together, these mechanisms reduce the lasing threshold by an order of magnitude compared to previous laser cavities with the same gain medium .

**4. Quantum dots as enhanced fluorescent probes**

Quantum dots (QDs) have become a major probe technology for fluorescence imaging. Their high photostability and brightness are superior to conventional organic fluorophores , and they improve fluorescence imaging due to photochemical stability and strong fluorescence output . QDs enable biological studies with extended spatiotemporal capabilities previously not possible , including multi-color and 3D tracking that provides new insights into cell signaling and protein trafficking , and in vivo tracking that allows observation of biological processes at the molecular level in whole animals . QD single-particle tracking (SPT) generates quantifiable dynamic information regarding diffusion . Limitations include their larger size (10–20 nm diameter) compared to organic fluorophores  and the challenge of achieving truly monovalent coupling in conjugation schemes .

When combined with PC substrates, QDs benefit from both the probe's intrinsic brightness and the substrate's enhancement. The PC-QD system achieves ~3000× enhancement in detected photon intensity , and the PC improves QD on-time from 15% to 85%, ameliorating blinking . Strong coupling to the PC modifies emission dynamics: it suppresses blinking and optical saturation , and the strong Purcell enhancement tremendously reduces saturation of the QD bright-state emission . The mechanism is that the strongly confined waveguide mode accelerates radiative decay, competing against the non-radiative dark-state transition .

**5. Application-level advances: biosensing and cell imaging**

*Digital-resolution biosensing.* Xiong et al. (2022) demonstrated a photonic-crystal-enhanced fluorescence platform for single-QD digital resolution biosensing. The combined mechanism yields a 23× excitation gain × 39× emission gain × 3.51× collection efficiency . The signal-to-noise ratio improved from <1 to 59.31 , and the detection limit improved by 10,000× versus an analog ensemble . The platform can discriminate a single base difference in a target miRNA within 10 minutes .

*Photonic-crystal enhanced microscopy (PCEM) for cell adhesion.* Chen et al. (2013) and Lidstone et al. (2011) developed PCEM, a label-free technique that monitors cell attachment without dyes or stains . It provides rich dynamic information about cell-surface attachment profiles over biologically relevant timescales , with spatial resolution sufficient to resolve filopodial extensions . The output signal is highly quantitative , with clearly visible boundaries of ~0.5 nm photonic wavelength shift (PWV) demonstrating sensitivity . Initial cell attachment is characterized by small round areas of PWV shifts . PC biosensors are fabricated from inexpensive materials and require only simple optics .

*Photonic resonator outcoupler microscopy (PROM).* Zhuo et al. (2018) used PROM to acquire dynamic images of focal adhesion (FA) development, a process that is difficult to image via conventional fluorescence .

**6. Design principles and open challenges**

The review by Xiong et al. (2023) distills several design principles: (i) careful consideration of photonic band structures (bandgap and resonances) is essential for PC design ; (ii) the PC bandgap arises from destructive interference of reflections at high/low index interfaces ; (iii) PCs support guided-mode resonances that channel internal light externally ; (iv) at resonant coupling, guided modes are excited within the PC ; (v) the absence of a complete photonic bandgap in opaline crystals limits their enhancement , though opal PCs effectively inhibit aggregation-promoted quenching of fluorophores . Photonic slabs (1D/2D PCs) are especially appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to good sensitivity, simplified optics, and substrate compatibility . Labeling analytes with fluorophores offers routes toward reduced limits of detection . PC structures can be integrated with appropriate optical components for futuristic applications , and PCCE biosensing can enable multiplexed sensing by tapping different resonances .

Open challenges include experimental artifacts during fabrication of PC substrates , the critical need to ensure only desired channels are exposed to functionalization , and the requirement for knowledge of the real and imaginary components of nanomaterials used for PC fabrication . The PCCE platform is considered promising for monitoring fluorescence dynamics .

**Summary of quantitative enhancements reported in the corpus:**

| Platform / Configuration | Enhancement | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| 2D PC (single-molecule) | 3000× |  |
| QDs on 2D PC (resonant) | 108.89 ± 4.09× |  |
| QDs on 2D PC (non-resonant) | 13.21 ± 0.26× |  |
| Near-field only (2D PC) | 8.24 ± 0.36× |  |
| PC + FP cavity (gold mirror) | 360× |  |
| 1D PC (Cy-5 streptavidin) | 60× |  |
| 3D opal PC ([Ru(dpp)₃]) | 320× |  |
| E-F-E CPhC (RhB) | ~1000× (thousand-fold) |  |
| E-F-E CPhC (additional over monolithic) | 5× |  |
| MHPC H-IV (additional over homogeneous) | 2.5× |  |
| PC-QD digital biosensing (combined) | 23× × 39× × 3.51× |  |
| PC-QD (detected photon intensity) | ~3000× |  |
| QD on-time (blinking suppression) | 15% → 85% |  |
| SNR (digital biosensing) | <1 → 59.31 |  |
| Detection limit improvement | 10,000× |  |

In summary, the recent research landscape for fluorescence enhancement in imaging is dominated by photonic-crystal engineering (2D slabs, 3D colloidal crystals, heterostructures, and cavity-coupled designs) that simultaneously addresses excitation, emission, and collection; plasmonic and hybrid photonic–plasmonic nanoantennas that provide extreme local field concentration; and advanced fluorescent probes (quantum dots) whose intrinsic properties complement the substrate enhancements. The field is moving toward integrated, label-free, and multiplexed platforms for biosensing and live-cell imaging, with the key open challenges being fabrication fidelity, functionalization selectivity, and the extension of enhancement to broader wavelength ranges and more complex biological environments.

answer_raw:
Recent research on enhancing fluorescence for imaging has advanced along several complementary axes: photonic-crystal (PC) substrates that reshape the local density of optical states, plasmonic nanoantennas that concentrate fields at the nanoscale, hybrid photonic–plasmonic and cavity-coupled architectures, and improved fluorescent probes (notably quantum dots). The corpus below synthesizes the principal mechanisms, quantitative gains, and application-level implications reported across these lines of work.

**1. Photonic-crystal-enhanced fluorescence (PCCE) — the dominant platform**

The central idea is to engineer a periodic dielectric structure whose bandgap or guided-mode resonances overlap with the excitation and/or emission wavelengths of the fluorophore, thereby (a) increasing the local excitation field, (b) modifying the radiative decay rate (Purcell effect), and (c) redirecting emitted photons into the collection cone. The review by Xiong et al. (2023) frames the field: only <30% of emitted light is typically detected even with sophisticated optical set-ups [1d427d01db113b], and the relative position of the excitation/emission maxima with respect to the PC's optical resonances "substantially influences" the nature and magnitude of enhancement [fe7901f10cbe05]. The review also notes a field-wide shift toward lossless dielectric platforms over metal plasmonics because of high energy dissipation in metals [6425b9ae33d3a9], and identifies the urgent need for sensor substrates that simultaneously enhance excitation, extraction, and quantum efficiency [cf9989a442a6ab].

*2D photonic crystals (photonic slabs).* A 2D PC produced a 3000-fold signal enhancement in a single-molecule detection context [fc7dc838f31d49]. In a separate study, quantum dots (QDs) on a 2D PC (period 300 nm, TiO₂ thickness 125 nm) showed a resonant fluorescence enhancement of 108.89 ± 4.09× versus an unpatterned surface, with a non-resonant control at 13.21 ± 0.26× and a near-field-only contribution of 8.24 ± 0.36× [612af8b1dedc23, c13c53f1407a51, 0e1fc7c4ce814f]. The mechanism was attributed to the combination of high-intensity near fields and Bragg scattering of coupled radiation out of the structure [802c0244088f75]. A key design insight from this work is the "doubly resonant" scheme: the PC is engineered so that leaky eigenmodes exist at both the absorption and emission wavelengths, so that external excitation of the leaky modes forms high-intensity near fields that efficiently excite the QDs, while coupling of the fluorescence to overlapping leaky modes plus Bragg scattering greatly reduces reabsorption [e3d82dd719d8d5, 70869a665dd761, 2df2e91e85eadc]. A low Q-factor (~92) of the extraction modes was found beneficial because it allows the coupled radiation to be scattered out rather than trapped [f6bdce6a99d29d, 8422f0db7b80b6]. The authors explicitly state that this doubly resonant scheme for enhancing QD emission had not been demonstrated before their report [242f5cde5751b4].

*PC coupled to an optical cavity.* Pokhriyal et al. (2013) demonstrated that coupling a 2D PC to an underlying Fabry–Perot cavity produces even higher evanescent fields on the PC surface than the PC alone [645399623c848d]. The coupled mode repeats every ~220 nm cavity length (≈λ_eff/2, constructive interference), and without the PC the structure behaves as a weak FP cavity without strong evanescent fields [6d881f213c8f0c, 4ec81ea6356884]. The underlying cavity coupled to the PC resonance increases the evanescent field intensity on the PC surface [74a0c77374c457]. The review cites a 360-fold enhancement achieved by coupling a PC leaky mode to an underlying Fabry–Perot cavity through a gold mirror [59f7b1fc5833f1].

*Leaky-mode-assisted extraction.* Ganesh et al. (2008) showed that the PC approach relies on coupling trapped light to free space via leaky modes created by the periodic structuring [6e6f24cb97d1c4]. Controlling the leaky-mode dispersion by tailoring PC properties redirects emitted light into preferred directions, enhancing collection efficiency [f7468959c67ed9]. The enhancement mechanism is resonant redirection of emitted radiation [8f92d48995e345].

*3D colloidal photonic crystals (CPhCs) and heterostructures.* Eftekhari et al. (2015) reported "anomalous" fluorescence enhancement from double heterostructure 3D colloidal PCs. The E-F-E (excitation–fluorescence–excitation) configuration acts as an etalon: two E layers reflect excitation light into the F layer, recycling it to increase excitation efficiency [3ba63537117f53]. The F layer is a CPhC with a partial bandgap overlapping the emission wavelength, acting as a strong resonator [fc35116c39b1ea]. The two E layers additionally form an optical resonator for the excitation light [1590e77a3393ae]. For Rhodamine B, the E-F-E structure achieved an additional 5-fold enhancement over monolithic E CPhCs [e43ba9ad7e16da], a 4.3-fold acceleration of emission dynamics [2aa50e235b47f9], and a ~6× improvement over monolithic CPhCs [4f3622f5e4cba2], reaching thousand-fold enhancement compared to a reference [16384dddd69e96]. The review cites a 320-fold luminescence enhancement of [Ru(dpp)₃] on 3D opal PCs [9f9edb7a8e9389] and a 60-fold increase for Cy-5-conjugated streptavidin on a 1D PC [aca90bf1e411d5].

*Multi-heterostructure colloidal PCs (MHPCs).* Zhang et al. (2018) introduced a "universal" fluorescence enhancement substrate based on multiple heterostructure PCs. The H-IV sample, formed by stacking homogeneous crystals with different polystyrene sphere sizes, exhibited a super-wide stopband from 280 to 650 nm [5d27949e9ae049], enabling simultaneous matching of excitation and emission wavelengths [aa3928d34e8339]. This yielded an additional 2.5-fold fluorescence enhancement over a homogeneous 245 nm film [f3b103cf33d874]. The mechanism involves an optical resonator environment from the stopband that couples with excitation light and scattering, improved via periodic dielectric constant modulation [0a4271f39cc0dd]. In contrast, homogeneous 160/200 nm crystals showed enhancement mainly from light scattering [35c3392385cee8], and the H-I sample did not display obvious bandgap broadening [642a46f80fb3c0]. The MHPC platform was demonstrated as a fluorescence sensing enhancement platform for Cr(VI) detection [4dc30150ef8a0b] and described as having "extraordinary ability to enhance FL signal for most commonly used fluorescent media" [911da95dbe585d].

*Purcell effect and lifetime modification.* Photonic crystals modify the radiative lifetime of emitters via redistribution of the photonic density of states [668ec516be8805, 44ef8c6219062c]. A dielectric PC produces quantum efficiency enhancement through the Purcell effect [651eef8bafbd10]. PC resonant modes provide photonic dispersion that controls the angular distribution of emitted photons [79c9fbb4fe5056].

**2. Plasmonic nanoantennas and hybrid photonic–plasmonic systems**

Plasmonic nanoantennas (e.g., gold bowtie antennas) create highly enhanced local electromagnetic fields when pumped resonantly [428c4b478178f7]. Kinkhabwala et al. (2009) demonstrated that bowtie antennas with smaller gaps (below 40 nm) produce higher local field strengths than larger-gap bowties and single triangles [00ffb6b04e24e6, da0090122dec44], and that the local field enhancement is highly dependent on the bowtie gap size [9ec55c35c83f6a]. A key finding is that low-quantum-efficiency emitters have much higher potential fluorescence brightness enhancements than high-QE emitters when placed on plasmonic nanoantennas [04c3d7e16ba17b]. Deep sub-wavelength confinement in these structures achieves a near-unity emission coupling factor despite the 2D isotropic nature of the emitters [b564049d857e08].

Hybrid photonic–plasmonic systems combine the field concentration of plasmonics with the low-loss guidance of photonics. A hybrid photonic coupling between nanoparticles and an underlying PC enhances fluorescence [6eb9c8884876e8]. The review notes that PCCE and PCEF (plasmonic fluorescence enhancement) platforms substantially differ in structural design and photonic response [0ebca26e54225c], and that novel nano-engineering methodologies combining both platforms can achieve further enhancement [8043c98ea70062].

**3. Enhanced emission and low-threshold lasing**

Zhen et al. (2013) demonstrated that optical resonances (exceptional points in non-Hermitian systems) modify light–matter interaction by enhancing absorption via pump coupling and improving extraction [98fbd2dc27b7b6]. The emission enhancement arises from two mechanisms: local excitation field enhancement and extraction rate enhancement [95c8a8faa1de99]. Together, these mechanisms reduce the lasing threshold by an order of magnitude compared to previous laser cavities with the same gain medium [c5e6a9575cf4e8].

**4. Quantum dots as enhanced fluorescent probes**

Quantum dots (QDs) have become a major probe technology for fluorescence imaging. Their high photostability and brightness are superior to conventional organic fluorophores [abecdc0a2dea9c], and they improve fluorescence imaging due to photochemical stability and strong fluorescence output [ea634692cc9396]. QDs enable biological studies with extended spatiotemporal capabilities previously not possible [82a781efa8ce0a], including multi-color and 3D tracking that provides new insights into cell signaling and protein trafficking [911db891d1e9a3], and in vivo tracking that allows observation of biological processes at the molecular level in whole animals [6d3019e1c3af62]. QD single-particle tracking (SPT) generates quantifiable dynamic information regarding diffusion [0415cc2de6591f]. Limitations include their larger size (10–20 nm diameter) compared to organic fluorophores [775d7c7499d484] and the challenge of achieving truly monovalent coupling in conjugation schemes [41d2b3482fb1f3].

When combined with PC substrates, QDs benefit from both the probe's intrinsic brightness and the substrate's enhancement. The PC-QD system achieves ~3000× enhancement in detected photon intensity [c127e1a12211a4], and the PC improves QD on-time from 15% to 85%, ameliorating blinking [dae29835eee2bf, e8d78607d133a9]. Strong coupling to the PC modifies emission dynamics: it suppresses blinking and optical saturation [7216ee33c9b46c], and the strong Purcell enhancement tremendously reduces saturation of the QD bright-state emission [5a2b4d0ff4a0fd]. The mechanism is that the strongly confined waveguide mode accelerates radiative decay, competing against the non-radiative dark-state transition [98fb65837d81a1].

**5. Application-level advances: biosensing and cell imaging**

*Digital-resolution biosensing.* Xiong et al. (2022) demonstrated a photonic-crystal-enhanced fluorescence platform for single-QD digital resolution biosensing. The combined mechanism yields a 23× excitation gain × 39× emission gain × 3.51× collection efficiency [c17f3456311dde]. The signal-to-noise ratio improved from <1 to 59.31 [59f69ccbac076a], and the detection limit improved by 10,000× versus an analog ensemble [e5d91ed09f16e2]. The platform can discriminate a single base difference in a target miRNA within 10 minutes [29202c469af623].

*Photonic-crystal enhanced microscopy (PCEM) for cell adhesion.* Chen et al. (2013) and Lidstone et al. (2011) developed PCEM, a label-free technique that monitors cell attachment without dyes or stains [993ea2117131aa]. It provides rich dynamic information about cell-surface attachment profiles over biologically relevant timescales [0852df2f29d4e7], with spatial resolution sufficient to resolve filopodial extensions [dda4e62e3d6b51]. The output signal is highly quantitative [92504150864166], with clearly visible boundaries of ~0.5 nm photonic wavelength shift (PWV) demonstrating sensitivity [d9df2c589c2fdd]. Initial cell attachment is characterized by small round areas of PWV shifts [46fd9cb7078c0e]. PC biosensors are fabricated from inexpensive materials and require only simple optics [81ccb9531cb759].

*Photonic resonator outcoupler microscopy (PROM).* Zhuo et al. (2018) used PROM to acquire dynamic images of focal adhesion (FA) development, a process that is difficult to image via conventional fluorescence [c20fbca99c8d28].

**6. Design principles and open challenges**

The review by Xiong et al. (2023) distills several design principles: (i) careful consideration of photonic band structures (bandgap and resonances) is essential for PC design [b2471ad89342b0]; (ii) the PC bandgap arises from destructive interference of reflections at high/low index interfaces [715d383b1f5dba]; (iii) PCs support guided-mode resonances that channel internal light externally [7955899e869348]; (iv) at resonant coupling, guided modes are excited within the PC [4fdbe5e019d4af]; (v) the absence of a complete photonic bandgap in opaline crystals limits their enhancement [d220a76dea909c], though opal PCs effectively inhibit aggregation-promoted quenching of fluorophores [b98828304af77b]. Photonic slabs (1D/2D PCs) are especially appealing for microfluidic biosensing due to good sensitivity, simplified optics, and substrate compatibility [f78a83bd28e5d3]. Labeling analytes with fluorophores offers routes toward reduced limits of detection [eb991f56d32304]. PC structures can be integrated with appropriate optical components for futuristic applications [4c974e528f03eb], and PCCE biosensing can enable multiplexed sensing by tapping different resonances [181eb02a53ef6d].

Open challenges include experimental artifacts during fabrication of PC substrates [bd43f9b32f5045], the critical need to ensure only desired channels are exposed to functionalization [d01607b85dcf46], and the requirement for knowledge of the real and imaginary components of nanomaterials used for PC fabrication [d78941d5534a8e]. The PCCE platform is considered promising for monitoring fluorescence dynamics [d8bbcaeadd9617].

**Summary of quantitative enhancements reported in the corpus:**

In summary, the recent research landscape for fluorescence enhancement in imaging is dominated by photonic-crystal engineering (2D slabs, 3D colloidal crystals, heterostructures, and cavity-coupled designs) that simultaneously addresses excitation, emission, and collection; plasmonic and hybrid photonic–plasmonic nanoantennas that provide extreme local field concentration; and advanced fluorescent probes (quantum dots) whose intrinsic properties complement the substrate enhancements. The field is moving toward integrated, label-free, and multiplexed platforms for biosensing and live-cell imaging, with the key open challenges being fabrication fidelity, functionalization selectivity, and the extension of enhancement to broader wavelength ranges and more complex biological environments.

question: How do exceptional points (EPs) in optical resonators enhance the sensitivity of sensors compared to traditional diabolic points (DPs) for detecting nanoparticles and biomolecules?
answer:
Exceptional points (EPs) in optical resonators enhance sensor sensitivity compared to traditional diabolic points (DPs) primarily through a distinct mathematical scaling of frequency splitting with respect to perturbation strength, which amplifies the response to minute changes in the environment. At an EP, which is defined as a branch singularity of a non-Hermitian system where at least two eigenmodes coalesce in both resonance frequencies and loss rates [7037d960b986ac][6b934d861df02c], the system exhibits square root singularities in its eigenvalues as a function of the complex interaction parameter [0a768f3024fbcf]. Consequently, when a system is perturbed about an EP, the resulting frequency splitting scales with the square root of the perturbation strength ($\sqrt{\varepsilon}$) [e4415ca5845e2d][7ecd63996df856]. In contrast, at a traditional diabolic point, the energy splitting scales linearly with the perturbation strength ($\varepsilon$) [7ecd63996df856][72ba424d7626d9]. This non-linear $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ dependence means that for sufficiently small perturbations, the frequency splitting at an EP is larger than that at a DP, even when the same perturbation Hamiltonian is applied, provided the square root term in the governing equation exceeds unity [86a1bdd0563689][679209f3fca17b]. This fundamental difference in scaling leads to a significant enhancement in sensitivity, as the derivative of the splitting with respect to the perturbation becomes increasingly large as the perturbation approaches zero, effectively amplifying the signal from minute changes in refractive index or mass [679209f3fca17b].

Quantitative comparisons between EP and DP sensors demonstrate this enhancement in both theoretical and experimental contexts. In a theoretical study of an EP microcavity sensor, the frequency splitting $|\Delta\Omega|$ was observed to be enhanced by a factor of 3 compared to the splitting at a diabolic point $|\Delta\Omega_{\mathrm{DP}}|$ [ceb3391c3f2656]. The paper states that there is no principle limitation on this enhancement factor, suggesting that the sensitivity can be further increased depending on the system parameters [ceb3391c3f2656]. Furthermore, the sensitivity is significantly enhanced when both frequency and linewidth splittings are measured, as the linewidths at the EP are increased to approximately $7|\Delta\Omega|$, which, while making it difficult to resolve the splitting individually, contributes to the overall sensitivity metric when combined with frequency data [44e41c9ec8bfaf][7f7380536bcd40][3a7717e57194f4]. In experimental plasmonic nanosensors, an EP system demonstrated a sensitivity of 4,821 nm per RIU (Refractive Index Unit) and was capable of detecting concentrations as low as $15\times10^{-12}$ g/L [4767ade7bef5db]. This performance was compared to a nanohole array sensor, which was reported with a sensitivity of 671 nm per RIU and detected sub-$10^{-6}$ g/L concentrations, and a hyperbolic metamaterial sensor with a sensitivity of 30,000 nm per RIU but a minimum detection limit of $2,440\times10^{-12}$ g/L [9cd4b902cba1c7][fd7ee58f2328a6]. These figures illustrate that while EP sensors may not always surpass the highest reported sensitivities of all alternative platforms in terms of nm/RIU, they offer superior detection limits for ultra-low concentrations due to the $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ scaling.

The detection of nanoparticles and biomolecules benefits from this enhanced sensitivity in specific ways. For biomolecule detection, such as IgG immunoassays, EP nanosensors exhibit larger resonance splitting than DP nanosensors for concentrations smaller than 1 fM [7fe436196f8058]. This advantage is consistent with the theoretical prediction that the EP nanosensor should exhibit larger splitting for small enough perturbations, whereas the DP nanosensor is expected to show larger splitting for large perturbations [325ef29acfa5dc]. In experiments where DP and EP sensors were fabricated on the same substrate with identical functionalization conditions and tested from 1,500 aM IgG, the EP sensor confirmed its higher sensitivity in the low-concentration regime [6955bacc455911][a745fd66031252]. For nanoparticle detection, the ultra-sensitivity of EPs allows for the distinction of particles with subtle differences. The trajectory of a particle near an EP closely resembles an ellipse, and the increase in the major axis of this ellipse can be several orders of magnitude larger than the increase in the particle radius [3e61507dd1ed59][72319dd9303f93]. This means that even a slight change in the refractive index can significantly alter the size and orientation of the ellipse, enabling the optical sorting and identification of particles that would be indistinguishable using traditional linear sensing methods [112995ed4b3c3a][c8563ec8273074][4d31294da78bb9].

However, the implementation and operation of EP sensors present certain challenges and limitations. The observation of EPs has historically been limited to wavelength-scaled systems subject to the diffraction limit, but plasmonic systems allow for the shrinking of wavelengths to electronic and molecular length scales, enabling subwavelength EP formation [88abea80207ff9][b41fdd9c710e46]. In plasmonic systems, EPs are formed through the hybridization of detuned resonances in multilayered structures, where detuning is implemented by symmetry breaking, such as using identical resonators in distinct environments [8cc1f26645c3cd][2c853770fd8d41]. A symmetric configuration cannot lead to EPs and instead results in Fano resonances; therefore, breaking the symmetry by making the resonators optically different is essential for EP formation [ae73259fd314ff][fb3392f3899fcc]. Despite these advancements, the implementation of EPs in subwavelength-scale systems like plasmonics remains challenging due to the difficulty of controlling loss and gain at such small scales [8274663ff3d917]. Additionally, fabrication errors can significantly impact performance; for instance, a fabrication error of $\pm5$ nm in the structural parameter $d_x$ at an EP can induce a mode splitting of approximately 6 THz, which is comparable to the shift induced by the biological linker, potentially complicating the interpretation of sensor signals [964f9ed1f11f5c]. Furthermore, while the optical sorting of particles is feasible near many EPs, it is not feasible near some EPs where the trajectories of different particles overlap, limiting the universality of the sorting application [f70d007248f0c9]. In specific experimental setups, such as the plasmonic EP nanosensor with a periodicity $P_y$ of 415 nm chosen to bring the system closer to the singularity, the EP singularity occurs around $\sim 243$ THz for $d_x$ of $\sim 134$ nm [81d24a788f3a19][644747daa4572f]. The consulted records did not surface the exact formulaic details for the sensitivity enhancement factor beyond the stated factor of 3 and the general $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ scaling, nor did they provide a comprehensive list of all biomolecule-specific detection results beyond the IgG immunoassay data.

answer_raw:
Exceptional points (EPs) in optical resonators enhance sensor sensitivity compared to traditional diabolic points (DPs) primarily through a distinct mathematical scaling of frequency splitting with respect to perturbation strength, which amplifies the response to minute changes in the environment. At an EP, which is defined as a branch singularity of a non-Hermitian system where at least two eigenmodes coalesce in both resonance frequencies and loss rates [7037d960b986ac][6b934d861df02c], the system exhibits square root singularities in its eigenvalues as a function of the complex interaction parameter [0a768f3024fbcf]. Consequently, when a system is perturbed about an EP, the resulting frequency splitting scales with the square root of the perturbation strength ($\sqrt{\varepsilon}$) [e4415ca5845e2d][7ecd63996df856]. In contrast, at a traditional diabolic point, the energy splitting scales linearly with the perturbation strength ($\varepsilon$) [7ecd63996df856][72ba424d7626d9]. This non-linear $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ dependence means that for sufficiently small perturbations, the frequency splitting at an EP is larger than that at a DP, even when the same perturbation Hamiltonian is applied, provided the square root term in the governing equation exceeds unity [86a1bdd0563689][679209f3fca17b]. This fundamental difference in scaling leads to a significant enhancement in sensitivity, as the derivative of the splitting with respect to the perturbation becomes increasingly large as the perturbation approaches zero, effectively amplifying the signal from minute changes in refractive index or mass [679209f3fca17b].

Quantitative comparisons between EP and DP sensors demonstrate this enhancement in both theoretical and experimental contexts. In a theoretical study of an EP microcavity sensor, the frequency splitting $|\Delta\Omega|$ was observed to be enhanced by a factor of 3 compared to the splitting at a diabolic point $|\Delta\Omega_{\mathrm{DP}}|$ [ceb3391c3f2656]. The paper states that there is no principle limitation on this enhancement factor, suggesting that the sensitivity can be further increased depending on the system parameters [ceb3391c3f2656]. Furthermore, the sensitivity is significantly enhanced when both frequency and linewidth splittings are measured, as the linewidths at the EP are increased to approximately $7|\Delta\Omega|$, which, while making it difficult to resolve the splitting individually, contributes to the overall sensitivity metric when combined with frequency data [44e41c9ec8bfaf][7f7380536bcd40][3a7717e57194f4]. In experimental plasmonic nanosensors, an EP system demonstrated a sensitivity of 4,821 nm per RIU (Refractive Index Unit) and was capable of detecting concentrations as low as $15\times10^{-12}$ g/L [4767ade7bef5db]. This performance was compared to a nanohole array sensor, which was reported with a sensitivity of 671 nm per RIU and detected sub-$10^{-6}$ g/L concentrations, and a hyperbolic metamaterial sensor with a sensitivity of 30,000 nm per RIU but a minimum detection limit of $2,440\times10^{-12}$ g/L [9cd4b902cba1c7][fd7ee58f2328a6]. These figures illustrate that while EP sensors may not always surpass the highest reported sensitivities of all alternative platforms in terms of nm/RIU, they offer superior detection limits for ultra-low concentrations due to the $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ scaling.

The detection of nanoparticles and biomolecules benefits from this enhanced sensitivity in specific ways. For biomolecule detection, such as IgG immunoassays, EP nanosensors exhibit larger resonance splitting than DP nanosensors for concentrations smaller than 1 fM [7fe436196f8058]. This advantage is consistent with the theoretical prediction that the EP nanosensor should exhibit larger splitting for small enough perturbations, whereas the DP nanosensor is expected to show larger splitting for large perturbations [325ef29acfa5dc]. In experiments where DP and EP sensors were fabricated on the same substrate with identical functionalization conditions and tested from 1,500 aM IgG, the EP sensor confirmed its higher sensitivity in the low-concentration regime [6955bacc455911][a745fd66031252]. For nanoparticle detection, the ultra-sensitivity of EPs allows for the distinction of particles with subtle differences. The trajectory of a particle near an EP closely resembles an ellipse, and the increase in the major axis of this ellipse can be several orders of magnitude larger than the increase in the particle radius [3e61507dd1ed59][72319dd9303f93]. This means that even a slight change in the refractive index can significantly alter the size and orientation of the ellipse, enabling the optical sorting and identification of particles that would be indistinguishable using traditional linear sensing methods [112995ed4b3c3a][c8563ec8273074][4d31294da78bb9].

However, the implementation and operation of EP sensors present certain challenges and limitations. The observation of EPs has historically been limited to wavelength-scaled systems subject to the diffraction limit, but plasmonic systems allow for the shrinking of wavelengths to electronic and molecular length scales, enabling subwavelength EP formation [88abea80207ff9][b41fdd9c710e46]. In plasmonic systems, EPs are formed through the hybridization of detuned resonances in multilayered structures, where detuning is implemented by symmetry breaking, such as using identical resonators in distinct environments [8cc1f26645c3cd][2c853770fd8d41]. A symmetric configuration cannot lead to EPs and instead results in Fano resonances; therefore, breaking the symmetry by making the resonators optically different is essential for EP formation [ae73259fd314ff][fb3392f3899fcc]. Despite these advancements, the implementation of EPs in subwavelength-scale systems like plasmonics remains challenging due to the difficulty of controlling loss and gain at such small scales [8274663ff3d917]. Additionally, fabrication errors can significantly impact performance; for instance, a fabrication error of $\pm5$ nm in the structural parameter $d_x$ at an EP can induce a mode splitting of approximately 6 THz, which is comparable to the shift induced by the biological linker, potentially complicating the interpretation of sensor signals [964f9ed1f11f5c]. Furthermore, while the optical sorting of particles is feasible near many EPs, it is not feasible near some EPs where the trajectories of different particles overlap, limiting the universality of the sorting application [f70d007248f0c9]. In specific experimental setups, such as the plasmonic EP nanosensor with a periodicity $P_y$ of 415 nm chosen to bring the system closer to the singularity, the EP singularity occurs around $\sim 243$ THz for $d_x$ of $\sim 134$ nm [81d24a788f3a19][644747daa4572f]. The consulted records did not surface the exact formulaic details for the sensitivity enhancement factor beyond the stated factor of 3 and the general $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ scaling, nor did they provide a comprehensive list of all biomolecule-specific detection results beyond the IgG immunoassay data.

question: In real research reading, scholar will search for relavent work or follow-up papers in order to get a more comprehensive understanding. Is there any work done to automate or assist in this process?
answer:
The process of automating or assisting scholars in searching for relevant work and follow-up papers is addressed in the consulted records primarily through two distinct technical approaches: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks designed to enhance the factuality and quality of large language models (LLMs) by grounding them in external search results, and specialized embedding benchmarks that evaluate the ability of models to retrieve related scientific documents. While the records do not surface a single unified system dedicated exclusively to "literature recommendation" in the traditional sense, they detail specific mechanisms and benchmarks that facilitate the identification of relevant papers and the integration of retrieved information into a coherent understanding.

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enhanced Understanding**

A significant body of work focuses on training LLMs to actively use search engines to ground their responses, thereby assisting in the comprehensive understanding of topics by retrieving relevant passages. SAIL (Search-Augmented Instruction Learning) is a framework that fine-tunes the LLaMA-7B model to utilize search engine results as grounding for its outputs [SAIL_Search-Augmented_Instruction_Learning]. By addressing the limitations of previous Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (RALMs) through the employment of real-world search engines, SAIL allows the model to concatenate retrieved passages directly into the language model's context [0098daa8eff428, 26cfcb32be59a1]. The system relies on non-differentiable retrievers, such as BM25, while focusing on improving the language model's ability to process this information [45e1c865e1cf45]. In terms of performance, SAIL-7B achieves 103% of ChatGPT's performance when search augmentation is applied [c944ed07f62183]. Without retrieval, SAIL-7B maintains a 49.5% average accuracy, which represents a 5.0% improvement over LLaMA-7B (44.5%) and an 8.6% improvement over Vicuna-7B (40.9%) [b44d705b333b58]. The integration of DuckDuckGo (DDG) search results further improves SAIL-7B by 2.8% on the OBQA dataset and by 1.2% on average . The search query construction in SAIL involves concatenating the instruction to form the query [537875be3cf698].

Similarly, Self-RAG is a framework designed to enhance the quality and factuality of an LLM through retrieval and self-reflection [Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_and_Critique, eb863110dbae2f]. Unlike systems that rely on fixed retrieval pipelines, Self-RAG trains a single arbitrary language model to adaptively retrieve passages on-demand [438de389ca4357]. The model generates specific "reflection tokens" to critique its own generation and the retrieved documents, including tokens for Retrieve, ISREL (Is Relevant), ISSUP (Is Supported), and ISUSE (Is Useful) [Self-RAG_Learning_to_Retrieve_Generate_and_Critique]. The Retrieve token outputs values from the set {yes, no, continue}, while the ISREL token outputs {relevant, irrelevant} [c11b5d5de1a9cb, b2265ee8af9319]. The paper states that Self-RAG outperforms ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on open-domain QA, reasoning, and factuality tasks [85374342b6cbe6]. Specifically, Self-RAG demonstrates significant gains in improving factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generation [6e5a7ca6b0cc01]. The demonstrated performance metrics for the Llama2-7B variant of Self-RAG include a Retrieve accuracy of 93.8, an ISSUP score of 93.5, an ISREL score of 80.2, and an ISUSE score of 73.5 [d997e6a4facd98, e3e4cb177fbe56, 3272b1df542eec, 81fec48451c93a]. The 13B variant of Self-RAG is reported to significantly outperform the baseline [b40cc834e2d5f2].

**Benchmarks for Scientific Paper Retrieval**

To specifically address the task of finding relevant or follow-up papers, the consulted records highlight specific tasks within the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) framework. MTEB is described as a framework that unifies datasets from different embedding tasks into a common, accessible evaluation framework, consisting of 58 datasets covering 112 languages from 8 embedding tasks, including bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, STS, and summarization [ca446ff36580c5, 50c9d16a8a1674]. The benchmark quantifies the gains provided by context-aware transformer models compared to word embedding models [ad552a14f5468f].

Within MTEB, three specific tasks are defined to evaluate the ability to retrieve related scientific papers:
1.  **SciDocsRR**: This task requires the model to retrieve the titles of other relevant papers given the title of a scientific paper [Improving_text_embeddings_with_large_language_models_#76950, Generative_Representational_Instruction_Tuning#172800].
2.  **SciDocsQ**: This task involves representing a scientific paper title to find the title and abstract of a scientific paper on PubMed that it has likely cited [Generative_Representational_Instruction_Tuning#184950].
3.  **SciDocsD**: This task requires representing the title and abstract of a scientific paper to find the title of another scientific paper on PubMed that likely cited it [Generative_Representational_Instruction_Tuning#184950].

These tasks directly model the scholarly process of identifying cited works and citing works, which are fundamental to following up on research.

**Supporting Infrastructure and Data Sources**

The effectiveness of these retrieval systems is supported by large-scale corpora and embedding models. For instance, the Dolma dataset is derived from the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC), providing a foundation for training models on scientific text [5b58f236f7e166]. Additionally, embedding models like NV-Embed are trained on tasks such as Biorxiv/Medrxiv clustering, which involves identifying the main category of papers based on titles and abstracts, a skill relevant to organizing and navigating literature [NV-Embed_Improved_Techniques_for_Training_LLMs_as_Generalist_Embedding_Models#94500]. Other approaches, such as Query Rewriting for RAG, utilize frozen LLMs like ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) and Vicuna-13B as readers to process retrieved information [af3d513ecd6a66]. In-context RALM methods also employ an open-book setting where retrieved passages are extended into the prompt to assist the model [b3e446f06889b5].

**Gaps in Consulted Records**

The consulted records did not surface specific papers dedicated exclusively to automated literature recommendation systems distinct from general RAG or embedding benchmarks. While the MTEB SciDocs tasks and RAG frameworks provide the technical mechanisms for retrieving and grounding information, the notes do not detail standalone "paper recommendation" algorithms or user-interface tools designed specifically for scholar workflow automation beyond the model-level capabilities described. Furthermore, the records did not provide detailed dossiers on the "reading comprehension work" entity or the specific structural details of the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus beyond its role as a data source for Dolma.
